SE9: The self-preservation Nine liked to brush aside unpleasant signals to avoid jeopardizing her familiar everyday comfort. Early, still-diffuse memory gaps are therefore often dismissed by her for an especially long time as harmless signs of aging, before family members notice the extent.
SO9: The social Nine usually put her own position in the group aside to preserve harmony, even when it concerned her own health. A necessary medical evaluation therefore often only enters her awareness late, once she can no longer even initiate it herself.
SX9: In merging with someone close, the sexual Nine often perceived their state more intensely than her own. It is therefore often exactly this person who first notices that something is changing in her memory and orientation – long before she herself speaks about it.
Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia are caused by misfolded proteins accumulating in the brain, genetic predisposition, age, and, in the case of vascular dementia, impaired blood flow – never by character traits or psychological patterns, and no subtype bears any share of responsibility. What does show up is simply that each of the 27 subtypes copes differently with the gradual loss of memory, independence, and familiar roles – some through maintained structure, others through the relationship to one particular close person. This knowledge does not replace medical and nursing care, but it can help family members and those affected understand why the same illness is experienced and carried so differently.

Parkinson's Disease (Psychosomatics Register · Nervous System & Psyche)
A progressive disease of the nervous system in which the loss of dopamine-producing cells increasingly slows, stiffens, and causes involuntary trembling in movement.
Definition: Parkinson's disease is a chronic, progressive neurodegenerative disease in which nerve cells that produce the neurotransmitter dopamine gradually die off in a specific area of the midbrain, the substantia nigra. The resulting dopamine deficiency leads to the classic motor core symptoms – resting tremor, muscle stiffness (rigidity), slowed movement (bradykinesia), and postural instability – as well as frequent non-motor accompanying symptoms such as impaired sense of smell, sleep disturbances, constipation, or depressive moods, which can precede the movement disorder by years in some cases. The exact cause remains unclear for most of those affected; it is thought to involve an interplay of genetic predisposition, aging processes in the nervous system, and possible environmental factors such as exposure to certain pesticides, with only a small proportion of cases traceable to clearly hereditary genetic changes.
Typical symptoms: Resting tremor, usually starting in one hand; Slowed, short-stepped movements (bradykinesia); Increased muscle tension and stiffness (rigidity); Increasingly stooped posture and gait and balance problems; Mask-like, less expressive facial expression; Quieter, more monotone speech; Non-motor accompanying symptoms such as loss of smell, sleep disturbances, or depressive mood
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Here too, the decisive clarification comes first: Parkinson's disease does not arise from a particular personality or a psychological pattern, but from the progressive death of dopamine-producing nerve cells in the midbrain – favored by genetic predisposition, the natural aging process of the nervous system, and, in a smaller proportion of cases, environmental influences. No subtype falls ill more often, less often, or more severely, and no one is responsible for their own trembling through behavior or character. What differs among the 27 subtypes is solely how a person deals with the progressive restriction of their freedom of movement, with visible symptoms in public, with growing dependence on help, and with the questions such a diagnosis raises about their own identity. This section describes exactly these different paths of coping – never a cause.
--- Type 1: When the hand no longer obeys ---
SE1: Precise, controlled movements mattered to the self-preservation One in everyday life; she usually corrected any inaccuracy immediately. A tremor she cannot stop no matter how hard she tries therefore confronts her directly with the limits of her otherwise so reliable self-control.
SO1: The social One wanted to be seen by those around her as a reliable, functioning role model; visible motor symptoms in public contradict this self-image, which is why she often tries at first to conceal them for as long as possible.
SX1: The sexual One discharges inner tension more immediately than other One variants, rather than suppressing it permanently. This more direct emotional processing can help her speak more openly about frustration with her own changing body, instead of carrying it silently.
--- Type 2: When hands can no longer help ---
SE2: Practical acts of help for others were a source of meaning to the self-preservation Two for years; when trembling or stiffness make exactly these tasks harder, it strikes not only her mobility but her self-understanding as a giver.
SO2: Slowed movement and growing fatigue can limit the social Two's accustomed availability to many people, which she often initially finds harder to accept than the physical symptoms themselves.
SX2: In her one important relationship, the sexual Two already engaged in mutual give and take. This openness often makes it easier for her to accept support with everyday tasks from exactly this person, rather than resisting it.
--- Type 3: When pace can no longer keep up ---
SE3: Efficiency and a brisk working pace mattered to the self-preservation Three for years; a disease that inevitably slows movement fundamentally challenges her accustomed functioning and demands a new understanding of productivity from her.
SO3: The social Three carefully cultivated her poised public appearance; a mask-like facial expression or visible tremor in public can therefore particularly unsettle her, because it involuntarily reveals what she never wanted to show.
SX3: The sexual Three already let her flawless facade drop earlier, but only in front of the one person who mattered to her. This already familiar protected space makes it easier for her to be more open about visible symptoms than about maintaining pure public perfection.
--- Type 4: When the body becomes a foreign place ---
SE4: Getting through everyday life toughly and without much fuss is familiar to the self-preservation Four, the counter-type; the progressive stiffness of Parkinson's nonetheless forces her to keep adjusting her quiet endurance to new, more visible limits.
SO4: The feeling of being different from others often accompanied the social Four even before any physical illness; a mask-like face that shows barely anything of her actual inner world on the outside can sharpen this inner contradiction between feeling and expression especially painfully.
SX4: The sexual Four usually sought intensity directly in encounter with others; slowed movement and reduced facial expression can make this direct emotional exchange harder, which is why she often looks for new ways to make closeness felt even without her accustomed means of expression.
--- Type 5: When the body restricts autonomy ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five secured her independence for years through a frugal, well-organized daily routine; increasing movement restrictions that make her dependent on others' help therefore strike directly at her central survival strategy.
SO5: Competence and a sharp mind mattered to the social Five for her place in the group; since thinking usually stays clear far longer than motor function in Parkinson's, she can often actively use this remaining mental sharpness to keep contributing despite physical limitations.
SX5: Genuine closeness and vulnerability, not purely withdrawing, is what the sexual Five already allowed herself within her one deep connection. This openness makes it easier for her to accept physical support from exactly this person, rather than isolating herself completely as the illness progresses.
--- Type 6: When the ground literally sways ---
SE6: Practically every conceivable risk in daily life was something the self-preservation Six prepared for in advance; gait and balance problems that bring a real risk of falling can fuel her underlying fear, but they can often be noticeably contained through concrete, well-planned adjustments to the living environment.
SO6: Reliable authorities and professional staff were where the social Six looked for security throughout her life; a clearly structured treatment plan with regular medical checkups often gives her more stability with Parkinson's than with less predictable disease courses of other kinds.
SX6: Rather than dwelling in worry, the sexual Six, the counter-type, usually acts decisively; this readiness to act often shows itself in Parkinson's in that she actively pursues movement therapy and training to hold the progression at bay for as long as possible.
--- Type 7: When spontaneity gets slowed down ---
SE7: Staying mobile and flexible always mattered greatly to the self-preservation Seven in everyday life; a disease that inevitably restricts movement and spontaneity fundamentally contradicts this core strategy and demands that she rediscover joy at a slower pace.
SO7: Putting her own exhaustion behind the group's needs was familiar to the social Seven, the counter-type; physical slowing that can no longer be masked forces her for the first time to take her own limits seriously instead of continuing to ignore them.
SX7: Focus on a single intense experience came more naturally to the sexual Seven than the constant pursuit of new stimulation; this capacity for focus helps her find intense, fulfilling moments in a smaller scope even with limited mobility.
--- Type 8: When the body shows weakness where strength once ruled ---
SE8: Physical strength and independence were things the self-preservation Eight watched over with great vigilance; visible trembling or diminishing power can feel like an attack on exactly the strength she has always defined herself by.
SO8: The social Eight consistently held the protective, strong position within her group; a disease that visibly restricts her mobility can call this protector role into question, until she learns that leadership remains possible even from a changed physical position.
SX8: Constant control gave way, earlier on, only in front of the one person the sexual Eight truly trusted; this practiced access to her own weakness eases her handling of progressive physical limitations compared with other Eight variants' permanent claim to control.
--- Type 9: When first signs are overlooked ---
SE9: Not jeopardizing her own everyday comfort always mattered more to the self-preservation Nine than any uncomfortable bodily signal; a slight tremor or changed handwriting is therefore often dismissed by her as a minor thing for a long time before an evaluation takes place.
SO9: Preserving harmony in the group always mattered more to the social Nine than her own health; a doctor's visit over first motor abnormalities therefore often only enters her awareness late, once others directly point it out to her.
SX9: The sexual Nine often perceived the wellbeing of her loved one more intensely than her own; it is often exactly this person who first notices subtle motor changes in her, long before she speaks about it herself.
Parkinson's disease is caused by the death of dopamine-producing nerve cells in the midbrain, favored by genetic predisposition, aging processes in the nervous system, and, in a smaller proportion of cases, environmental influences – never by character traits or psychological patterns. What does show up is simply that each of the 27 subtypes copes differently with the progressive restriction of movement, pace, and expression – some through active training, others through the relationship to one particular trusted person or a newly found patience with themselves. This knowledge does not replace neurological treatment, but it can help, alongside it, to understand why people respond so differently to the same diagnosis.

Epilepsy (Psychosomatics Register · Nervous System & Psyche)
A neurological disease involving recurrent seizures, in which nerve cells in the brain suddenly discharge in an uncontrolled, synchronized way.
Definition: Epilepsy is a neurological disease characterized by recurrent epileptic seizures – sudden, uncontrolled electrical discharges of groups of nerve cells in the brain that can take very different forms depending on the brain region affected: from brief absence seizures with a pause in consciousness, through focal seizures with isolated motor or sensory symptoms, to generalized tonic-clonic seizures with loss of consciousness and convulsions throughout the body. The causes are varied: genetic predisposition, brain damage from accidents, strokes, infections, or tumors, brain malformations, or – in a considerable proportion of those affected – no clear cause can be found despite thorough diagnostic workup. With appropriate medication, the majority of those affected achieve good seizure control or complete freedom from seizures.
Typical symptoms: Sudden brief lapses in consciousness (absence seizures); Involuntary jerking of individual body parts or the whole body; Temporary speech, vision, or sensory disturbances during a focal seizure; Loss of consciousness with falling and generalized convulsions; Unusual sensations or a warning feeling (aura) before some seizures; Confusion, exhaustion, or sore muscles after a seizure; In some forms, tongue biting or involuntary loss of bladder control during the seizure
Emergency notice: An epileptic seizure is a medical emergency requiring an immediate call to emergency services if it lasts longer than five minutes, or if several seizures occur in a row without the person fully regaining consciousness in between (status epilepticus), if it is the person's very first seizure ever, if the seizure is accompanied by an injury, a fall from height, occurs in water, or involves breathing difficulties, or if the person does not regain consciousness within a few minutes after the seizure. During a seizure: protect the person from injury, do not put anything in their mouth, if possible move them into the stable recovery position, and time the seizure.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Here too, the most important thing comes first: epilepsy does not arise from a particular personality or a psychological pattern, but from neurological causes – genetic predisposition, brain damage, a malformation, or, in many of those affected, with no findable cause at all. No subtype falls ill more often or bears responsibility for their own seizures. What differs among the 27 subtypes is solely how a person lives with the unpredictability of a seizure that can in principle strike at any time, how they handle the often stigmatized public image of epilepsy, how they involve family and their surroundings, and how they balance safety precautions with the wish for as normal an everyday life as possible. This section describes exactly these different paths of coping – never a cause.
--- Type 1: When control becomes impossible in the moment of a seizure ---
SE1: Control over her own body and its course mattered centrally to the self-preservation One in everyday life; a seizure that suspends exactly this control without any warning can therefore shake her especially deeply and intensify her drive toward strict medication compliance and precaution even further.
SO1: Being seen publicly as reliable and composed mattered to the social One throughout her life; the worry of having a seizure precisely in public and losing control there can weigh on her more heavily than the medical risk itself.
SX1: The sexual One discharges her feelings more immediately than other One variants; this more direct expression can help her speak more openly about fear of the next seizure, instead of carrying it silently the way other One variants tend to.
--- Type 2: When worrying about others becomes worrying about oneself ---
SE2: Attending to others rather than even naming her own needs was more familiar to the self-preservation Two for years; consistently keeping up regular medication and self-care for her own sake can therefore be harder for her than for almost anyone else.
SO2: Being available for others at all times mattered to the social Two; the need to let those close to her know about her condition and how to act in an emergency is often experienced by her not as a burden but as a new way of forging connection.
SX2: The sexual Two already lived mutual care rather than one-sided giving in her one important relationship; making exactly this person her trusted contact for emergencies therefore comes more easily to her than the purely giving role adopted by other Two variants.
--- Type 3: When a seizure shatters the image before others ---
SE3: Efficient functioning in everyday life mattered to the self-preservation Three; a seizure that abruptly pulls her out of whatever she is doing can therefore alarm her less because of the physical symptoms than because of the sudden interruption of her capability.
SO3: Poise in front of others was something the social Three cultivated with great care; a seizure that strikes precisely in public, over which she has no control at all, is among the situations that can most directly call this poised image into question.
SX3: The sexual Three already practiced allowing weakness earlier, but only in front of the one person who mattered to her; this already familiar retreat can help her speak openly about the illness, unlike many other Three variants who try to keep it hidden.
--- Type 4: When the seizures shape one's own story ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four, the counter-type, usually reacts to burdens tersely and functionally rather than with complaint; she often deals with an epilepsy diagnosis at first in a functional rather than emotional way too, which easily hides her actual unsettlement from family members.
SO4: A sense of being different from others often accompanied the social Four even before any diagnosis; a disease that genuinely carries stigma and misunderstanding can confirm this sense of otherness in a painfully concrete way, but it can also become an occasion to speak openly about her own experience.
SX4: Direct encounter mattered more to the sexual Four than any retrospection; the unusual, often intense warning feeling (aura) that precedes some seizures is sometimes processed by her as her own, hardly communicable experience that sets her apart from other people with the condition.
--- Type 5: When the unpredictable escapes knowledge ---
SE5: Knowledge and forward planning were how the self-preservation Five secured her independence over the years; a disease whose next seizure is fundamentally unpredictable slips out of reach of this strategy, which is why she often reads especially thoroughly about triggers, warning signs, and emergency measures to regain a sense of control.
SO5: Competence and specialized knowledge mattered to the social Five for her place in the group; thoroughly informing herself about her particular form of epilepsy can help her meet medical staff and family on equal footing, instead of experiencing herself purely as a patient.
SX5: Emotional openness already came earlier for the sexual Five within her one deep connection; confiding her fear of the next seizure to exactly this person comes easier to her than to the wider circle, from whom she tends to conceal the condition instead.
--- Type 6: When unpredictability hits her core fear ---
SE6: Taking precautions against practically every conceivable risk has always mattered to the self-preservation Six; a disease whose next seizure by definition gives no warning can first noticeably intensify her underlying anxiety, before a well-rehearsed emergency system with those around her and her medication restores a sense of security.
SO6: The social Six oriented herself toward reliable authorities to find security; close, well-coordinated care from neurology together with an informed social circle often gives her more stability with epilepsy than trying to manage everything alone.
SX6: Acting boldly and immediately comes more naturally to the sexual Six, the counter-type, than endless rumination; this attitude often shows itself in epilepsy in that she deals openly with the diagnosis and actively takes precautions, instead of letting fear of the next seizure hold her back.
--- Type 7: When spontaneity needs new caution ---
SE7: Keeping as many options open as possible always mattered more to the self-preservation Seven than doing without; the necessity of consistently avoiding triggers such as sleep deprivation or alcohol contradicts this core strategy, which is why this new discipline is often harder for her than for other subtypes.
SO7: Acting selflessly rather than self-centeredly shaped the social Seven, the counter-type, for years; consistently keeping up regular medication and precautions for her own sake demands a self-care from her that she finds easier to extend to others than to herself.
SX7: Focus rather than constant seeking of stimulation was already more familiar to the sexual Seven than to other Seven variants; this ability makes it easier for her to see necessary precautions as a conscious part of a fulfilled rather than restricted everyday life.
--- Type 8: When a seizure visibly takes control away ---
SE8: Vigilance over her own physical control is second nature to the self-preservation Eight; a seizure during which she inevitably becomes exposed to others can therefore be experienced as an especially deep loss of control, which she often tries afterward to compensate for with even stricter medication discipline.
SO8: Being strong and protective for her group always mattered to the social Eight; a seizure in front of others, in which she suddenly needs protection herself, temporarily turns this role upside down, until she learns that strength can also lie in accepting help at the right moment.
SX8: Maintaining control throughout, except in front of the one truly trusted person, was already familiar to the sexual Eight; making exactly this person her closest confidant in dealing with the condition comes easier to her than being open with the wider circle.
--- Type 9: When early signs go unheeded for too long ---
SE9: Neglecting physical warning signs is among the familiar patterns of the self-preservation Nine; unusual brief blackouts or a diffuse warning feeling are therefore sometimes dismissed by her as a minor thing for a long time, before a first medical evaluation follows.
SO9: Holding herself back within the group was familiar to the social Nine for years; a doctor's visit after a first, perhaps unnoticed seizure therefore often only comes to the fore once someone from her circle points it out directly.
SX9: Merging with a loved one shaped the sexual Nine often more strongly than her own self-perception; it is often exactly this person who notices a first seizure and is the one who actually initiates the necessary evaluation.
Epilepsy is caused by genetic predisposition, brain damage, a malformation, or, in many of those affected, remains without any findable cause at all – never by character traits or psychological patterns. What does show up is simply that each of the 27 subtypes deals differently with the fundamental unpredictability of a seizure, with safety precautions, and with how their own surroundings respond – some through thorough knowledge, others through the close bond to one particular trusted person or a deliberately open stance. This knowledge does not replace neurological treatment, but it can help, alongside it, to understand why people respond so differently to the same diagnosis.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (Psychosomatics Register · Nervous System & Psyche)
A rare, rapidly progressing disease of the nervous system in which the nerve cells for voluntary muscle movement increasingly die, while the mind usually stays clear.
Definition: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rare, incurable, and usually rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disease in which the motor nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord responsible for voluntary muscle control gradually die off. The result is progressive muscle weakness and wasting that can eventually affect almost all voluntarily controlled muscles – from the limbs to the muscles used for speech and swallowing to the respiratory muscles – while sensory perception, bladder and bowel function, and, in the large majority of those affected, cognitive function remain intact. In about 90 percent of cases, ALS occurs with no discernible family history; in around 10 percent, an inherited, genetically caused form is present. The precise triggering mechanisms are still not fully understood despite intensive research; an interplay of genetic predisposition, disturbed protein metabolism in nerve cells, and, in a small proportion of cases, possible environmental factors is discussed.
Typical symptoms: Progressive muscle weakness, usually starting in one hand, arm, or leg; Muscle twitching (fasciculations) and increasing muscle wasting; Speech and swallowing difficulties when the muscles of the mouth and throat are involved; Increasing respiratory weakness as the disease progresses; Preserved sensory perception and, for most of those affected, preserved cognitive function; Muscle cramps and increased reflexes; Emotional lability with involuntary laughing or crying in some forms of the disease
Emergency notice: Call emergency services immediately for sudden severe shortness of breath or risk of choking from swallowing difficulty. Because ALS progressively weakens the respiratory muscles, close attachment to a specialized ALS center is important, so that support such as assisted ventilation, feeding tubes, and an advance directive can be discussed in good time, before an acute crisis occurs.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Here too, the most important thing comes first: ALS does not arise from a particular personality, from strength or weakness of character, or from a psychological pattern, but from the progressive death of motor nerve cells – caused by genetic predisposition, disturbed protein metabolism in nerve cells, and, in a small proportion of cases, possible environmental factors. No subtype carries a higher risk, and no one is responsible for this disease through their own behavior or thinking. What differs among the 27 subtypes is solely how a person lives with the rapid, often especially cruel contrast of a mind that usually stays clear while the body increasingly fails to obey – how they communicate once speaking is no longer possible, how they cope with growing complete dependence on family and care, and what role they must renegotiate in their closest relationships. This section describes these different ways of coping – never a cause, and never a judgment on how someone handles this especially difficult diagnosis.
--- Type 1: When the will remains but the body no longer follows ---
SE1: Disciplined functioning in everyday life was the foundation of the self-preservation One's self-respect for years; that her will to control remains unbroken with ALS while her body increasingly can no longer follow it is among the bitterest experiences of this disease for her.
SO1: Her reputation as a reliable, functioning role model carried the social One for years; increasingly communicating through technical aids or assistance rather than speaking and acting herself demands an entirely new definition of reliability from her.
SX1: The sexual One already expressed her feelings more immediately than other One variants; this more direct emotional access can help her express both closeness and anger genuinely through alternative means of communication even as speech progressively fails, rather than falling silent inwardly.
--- Type 2: When total dependence reverses the giving role ---
SE2: Allowing her own neediness was far harder for the self-preservation Two for decades than caring for others; the complete dependence on others' help that ALS makes unavoidable represents one of the most radical reversals of her entire life pattern.
SO2: The social Two often measured her worth by being indispensable to many people at once; when she can increasingly no longer give but only receive, she is often helped by the realization that her mere presence and her gaze continue to create connection, even without active doing.
SX2: The sexual Two already practiced openness to dependency earlier within her one important relationship; this already lived experience often carries her when exactly this person becomes her central caregiver, while other Two variants must learn to receive help far more painfully.
--- Type 3: When one's own capability irreversibly fades ---
SE3: Her practical competence was proof of her own worth to the self-preservation Three for years; the rapid loss of motor abilities typical of ALS therefore hits her especially hard, because it leaves her no time to gradually get used to a new self-image.
SO3: Professional and public success often shaped the social Three's self-image; some people with ALS find here an unexpected new role in making their illness visible publicly, thereby continuing to accomplish something that reaches beyond their own physical capability.
SX3: Long before the diagnosis, the sexual Three already knew this one protected space with her most important person, where weakness was allowed; it can help her continue to experience herself as lovable amid growing need for care, instead of defining herself solely by lost abilities.
--- Type 4: When inner experience stays intense while expression fades ---
SE4: Quiet, functional endurance characterizes the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, over the years; with ALS it nonetheless brings her to a hard limit, once physical exhaustion at some point no longer allows for functional coping and open support becomes unavoidable.
SO4: Her own, often intensely experienced inner world was central to the social Four's self-understanding; when speech and facial expression become increasingly restricted by the disease, the loss of being able to show this inner world outwardly can weigh more heavily than the physical loss itself.
SX4: The sexual Four usually lived intensity in direct encounter; when progressive speech and movement restrictions take away this direct channel of expression, she often seeks new, equally intense ways of closeness – through eye contact, touch, or assisted communication – rather than withdrawing.
--- Type 5: When a clear mind stays trapped in a silenced body ---
SE5: Her thinking was always the self-preservation Five's safest place; that the mind usually stays clear with ALS while the body increasingly fails to obey hits her at an especially paradoxical point – her greatest strength remains intact but becomes increasingly hard to communicate.
SO5: Her specialized knowledge earned the social Five recognition within the group for years; assistive communication technology that still allows thoughts to be conveyed precisely even in advanced illness can help her continue contributing to the group despite physical limitations.
SX5: Emotional openness was already practiced by the sexual Five earlier within her one deep connection; this familiarity often carries her when words become slower or no longer possible at all – a glance or a gesture is then enough for an understanding that other Five variants have less often built with those around them.
--- Type 6: When security remains only within the closest circle ---
SE6: Leaving nothing unprepared always mattered to the self-preservation Six in everyday life; an ALS diagnosis with its usually rapid, clearly foreseeable progression can initially plunge her into deep fear, but it also gives her the chance to take concrete precautions early – from an advance directive to communication aids – which gives her back a measure of agency.
SO6: The social Six found security throughout life above all through reliable authorities; close attachment to a specialized ALS center with clear points of contact gives her dependable stability, at least in the structure of her care, in the face of a disease with no prospect of cure.
SX6: Decisiveness rather than rumination characterizes the sexual Six, the counter-type, in dealing with fear; this attitude often shows itself in ALS in that she actively takes part in planning her own care and speaks openly about the course ahead, instead of suppressing it.
--- Type 7: When no escape route remains open ---
SE7: No door was ever supposed to close permanently for the self-preservation Seven; a rapidly progressing disease that takes away practically every physical way out is among the hardest diagnoses for her to bear and demands a radically new definition of joy from her.
SO7: Letting her own limits disappear behind the group's was familiar to the social Seven, the counter-type, for years; with ALS the disease forces her for the first time to place her own limits and needs unmistakably at the center, which she initially experiences as unfamiliar but often, over time, also as liberating.
SX7: Being fully absorbed in the present moment came more easily to the sexual Seven than to many other Seven variants; this ability can help her still find dense, meaningful moments with those close to her even as her possibilities narrow, rather than mourning what is lost.
--- Type 8: When total need for help becomes unavoidable ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight watched over her physical strength and independence with great vigilance; the complete need for care that ALS makes unavoidable is among the most radical conceivable challenges to her self-image and demands an entirely new definition of strength from her, one found in consciously allowing help.
SO8: Being the protector of her group was core to the social Eight's self-image; when she herself becomes the one who must be fully protected and cared for, she often finds it easier to accept this reversal if she continues to be seen as a source of orientation – through clear decisions, bearing, and will – even without physical capability.
SX8: The sexual Eight already opened up with her vulnerability earlier, though only to the one truly trusted person; this already practiced access often carries her more easily through the complete dependence ALS brings than other Eight variants who have never before allowed vulnerability.
--- Type 9: When early weakness is played down for too long ---
SE9: Early physical warning signs are easily forgotten by the self-preservation Nine as long as everyday comfort remains intact; a first, still inconspicuous weakness in a hand or leg is therefore often dismissed by her for an unusually long time as tension or everyday tiredness, before a thorough neurological workup follows.
SO9: Putting her own concerns behind the group's belonged to the social Nine's pattern for a long time; a necessary medical evaluation of first motor abnormalities correspondingly often only comes to the fore once someone close to her insists on it.
SX9: The sexual Nine's own perception often steps behind that of her loved one; with ALS this particular closeness is at the same time one of the greatest supports over the course of the illness, because it is exactly this person who usually senses earliest when help is needed and who remains at her side the longest.
ALS is caused by the progressive death of motor nerve cells, favored by genetic predisposition and disturbed protein metabolism in nerve cells, and in a small proportion of cases also by environmental factors – never by character traits, willpower, or its supposed absence. What does show up is simply that each of the 27 subtypes deals differently with the especially difficult contrast between a clear mind and fading physical capability – some through early, decisive preparation, others through the sustaining closeness of one particular trusted person or a newly found definition of strength in consciously allowing help. This knowledge does not replace specialized medical and nursing care, but it can help family members and those affected understand why the same illness is experienced and carried so differently.

Liver Cancer (Psychosomatics Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the liver that usually develops on the basis of an already damaged liver and causes few symptoms for a long time.
Definition: Liver cancer (most commonly hepatocellular carcinoma) is a malignant tumor arising from liver tissue itself – distinct from liver metastases of other cancers. By far the most common precursor is a chronically damaged liver: cirrhosis caused by chronic hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection, longstanding significant alcohol use, or a non-alcoholic fatty liver, often linked to overweight and diabetes. Other risk factors include certain mold toxins (aflatoxins) in contaminated food and rare inherited metabolic disorders such as hemochromatosis. Because the liver can compensate for a long time, the tumor often remains unnoticed until an advanced stage. Treatment ranges from surgical partial removal or liver transplantation to local procedures such as ablation or embolization, targeted drugs, and immunotherapy; the prognosis depends heavily on the stage and the condition of the remaining liver.
Typical symptoms: Pressure or pain in the upper right abdomen; Unexplained weight loss; Loss of appetite and feeling full quickly; Yellowing of skin and eyes (jaundice); Increasing abdominal girth from fluid buildup; Persistent tiredness and weakness; Itching over the whole body
Emergency notice: Jaundice, a rapidly increasing abdominal girth, severe pain in the upper right abdomen, or unexplained weight loss should be checked by a doctor promptly. With known liver cancer accompanied by confusion, vomiting blood, black stool, or high fever, seek medical help immediately.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
As with all oncological conditions in this compass, it applies here explicitly: psychological patterns do not cause cancer. Liver cancer usually develops on the basis of an already damaged liver – through chronic hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection, longstanding alcohol use, a fatty liver related to overweight and diabetes, or rare inherited metabolic disorders – factors that are not directly connected to a person's personality. Anyone who receives this diagnosis bears no character-based blame for it, even if earlier lifestyle habits may have played a role – assigning blame helps no one. What follows instead is this: how differently people, depending on subtype, cope with the often double burden of underlying liver disease and cancer diagnosis, how they wrestle with or suppress their own part in the history leading up to it, how they experience treatment decisions such as a possible transplant, and how their relationship to their body and to loved ones changes in the process. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how diagnosis, treatment, and uncertainty are handled – not in how the illness arises.
--- Type 1: Between Self-Reproach and Composure ---
SE1: If earlier lifestyle choices really did play a part in the illness, the self-preservation One tends toward a harsh inner reckoning with herself that goes far beyond what is medically useful.
SO1: It matters to the social One that people around her don't jump to explaining the diagnosis with an assumed unhealthy lifestyle, so she often deliberately frames the causes factually before rumors can take hold.
SX1: Anger over a possibly avoidable precondition like untreated hepatitis is directed outward openly by the sexual One, rather than disciplined and contained the way other One variants tend to handle it.
--- Type 2: Caring for Others Despite Their Own Exhaustion ---
SO2: Her wider family network is kept actively together by the social Two even during treatment – she organizes visits and support for others while her own exhaustion from the liver disease takes a back seat.
SE2: Small, concrete acts of help in daily life – preparing food, coordinating appointments – remain a way for the self-preservation Two to still feel useful, even as fatigue advances.
SX2: Openly asking for care as jaundice and weakness increase comes more easily to the sexual Two within the one relationship that matters most to her – more so than for other Two variants.
--- Type 3: Staying Capable Despite a Weakened Liver ---
SE3: Her stamina at work is something the self-preservation Three wants to keep proving for as long as possible despite mounting exhaustion from the liver disease, before admitting she needs a break.
SX3: Her sense of her own body wavers when jaundice or abdominal swelling becomes visible – toward the one important person, the sexual Three allows this uncertainty to show more readily than in public.
SO3: Outwardly, the social Three keeps presenting herself as controlled and successful even as the illness progresses, while itching, tiredness, and worry about the prognosis stay largely invisible.
--- Type 4: An Illness With a Double Face ---
SO4: That liver cancer is often linked to preconditions like alcohol use can deepen old feelings of being misunderstood in the social Four, since she feels additionally judged on top of her suffering.
SE4: Fear and exhaustion from the illness are usually carried by the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, in a tough, functional way rather than expressed dramatically as would otherwise be typical for her type.
SX4: Even the shame some connect to a possible history of alcohol use or hepatitis is revealed by the sexual Four to the one person she feels most deeply bonded to, rather than hidden away.
--- Type 5: Understanding What Is Happening in the Liver ---
SO5: In specialist forums or with fellow patients, the social Five prefers exchanging views on liver values, embolization procedures, and study data rather than putting her own emotional experience of the diagnosis in the foreground.
SE5: Before committing to a treatment decision such as a possible transplant, the self-preservation Five usually gets a precise overview of waiting lists, success rates, and alternatives.
SX5: Even fear of the disease progressing is opened up by the sexual Five toward the one deep connection, rather than kept at arm's length the purely factual way other Five variants tend to manage it.
--- Type 6: Trust on Uncertain Ground ---
SO6: Several medical opinions and advice from support groups are often gathered by the social Six before she trusts a treatment decision like being listed for transplant – deciding alone isn't enough for her.
SE6: Regular checks of liver values and imaging are attended conscientiously by the self-preservation Six, yet every appointment still triggers fresh worry about the disease progressing.
SX6: Uncertainty about her own prognosis is met by the sexual Six, the counter-type, with decisive action, such as quickly agreeing to a recommended treatment, rather than getting lost in doubt.
--- Type 7: Between Distraction and Forced Rest ---
SO7: Dietary restrictions, alcohol abstinence, follow-up appointments – the social Seven, the counter-type, keeps to all of it with unusual discipline, even though the restriction weighs on her inwardly.
SE7: Keeping several possible treatment paths in view at once gives the self-preservation Seven the feeling of not being trapped – a single binding treatment track can instead feel confining.
SX7: Distraction gives way, for once, when the sexual Seven faces the one decisive conversation about transplant or prognosis, rather than retreating into it as other Seven variants tend to.
--- Type 8: Reclaiming Control Over Her Own Body ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight wants to keep decision-making authority over diet, alcohol abstinence, and the treatment plan, and reacts with irritation when doctors give orders instead of laying out options.
SO8: The protective, dependable figure is a role the social Eight continues playing in front of her family even as the liver disease advances, usually keeping her own exhaustion and worry hidden.
SX8: Her fear about her own body and the prognosis is opened up by the sexual Eight toward the one person she trusts, rather than demonstrating strength throughout.
--- Type 9: Finding Her Own Voice in Treatment ---
SE9: Early warning signs like persistent tiredness or loss of appetite are often blocked out for a long time by the self-preservation Nine within her familiar routine, until a clear medical finding forces her to confront it.
SO9: Surgery, embolization, or transplant listing decisions tend to see the social Nine defer to the doctors' recommendation or the family's stance without staking out a clear preference of her own.
SX9: How much a partner or family suffers under the diagnosis is often noticed more clearly by the sexual Nine than her own exhaustion, causing her own needs to easily get lost in treatment decisions.
Liver cancer usually develops on the basis of an already damaged liver – through chronic viral infections, longstanding alcohol use, fatty liver, or rare inherited causes – never through character traits or psychological patterns. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes copes differently with the often double burden of underlying illness and cancer diagnosis – some through knowledge and control, others through withdrawal, caring for others, or unaccustomed openness toward someone close. This knowledge does not replace oncological treatment, but can help, alongside it, to understand why people respond so differently to the same diagnosis.

Bladder Cancer (Psychosomatics Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the bladder lining that usually appears in older age and often first shows itself as painless blood in the urine.
Definition: Bladder cancer (most commonly urothelial carcinoma) is a malignant tumor arising from the lining of the bladder. By far the largest risk factor is smoking, which contributes to a substantial share of all cases. Other recognized causes include longstanding occupational exposure to certain chemicals (for example in the dye, rubber, or textile industries), chronic bladder irritation, and, in some parts of the world, certain parasitic infections. Risk rises with age, and men are affected considerably more often than women. A typical first warning sign is painless blood in the urine, which is easily overlooked or misread. Depending on how deeply it has grown, treatment ranges from endoscopic removal of superficial tumors to bladder instillation therapy to surgical removal of the bladder with construction of a urinary diversion, along with chemotherapy and immunotherapy; the prognosis depends crucially on how deeply the tumor has already grown into the bladder wall.
Typical symptoms: Painless blood in the urine; Frequent urge to urinate despite passing little urine; Burning or pain when urinating without an identifiable infection; Pain in the lower back on one side; Unexplained weight loss; Persistent tiredness
Emergency notice: Blood in the urine, even when it is painless and disappears again, should be checked by a doctor promptly. With known bladder cancer accompanied by severe pain, inability to urinate, high fever, or marked shortness of breath, seek medical help immediately.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
As with all oncological conditions in this compass, it applies here explicitly: psychological patterns do not cause cancer. Bladder cancer arises mainly from smoking, longstanding occupational exposure to certain chemicals, chronic bladder irritation, age, and chance – factors that are not directly connected to a person's personality. Anyone who receives this diagnosis bears no character-based blame for it. What follows instead is something else: how differently people, depending on subtype, react to an initially inconspicuous symptom like painless blood in the urine, how they talk about a possible bladder removal and a changed urinary diversion, how burdensome the loss of familiar bodily control feels to them, and how their relationship to shame, closeness, and daily life changes through treatment and follow-up care. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how diagnosis, treatment, and uncertainty are handled – not in how the illness arises.
--- Type 1: Precision Against Uncertainty ---
SE1: Her cystoscopies and instillation appointments are planned by the self-preservation One with great care, while inwardly she wrestles with not having taken an early warning sign like blood in the urine seriously right away.
SO1: Before telling those around her about the diagnosis, the social One wants to be fully informed about treatment options such as a possible urinary diversion, so as to come across as factual rather than alarming.
SX1: A diagnostic delay she considers avoidable leaves the sexual One openly frustrated, and she says so bluntly and right away, unlike the contained, disciplined manner other One variants tend to show.
--- Type 2: Shame and Caring in Alternation ---
SX2: About the question of a urinary stoma, which feels shameful to her, the sexual Two speaks openly with the one person who matters most to her, rather than keeping it quiet.
SE2: Even with a changed urinary diversion, the self-preservation Two keeps organizing practical help for others in daily life, often overriding her own exhaustion after the surgery.
SO2: Among the wider circle beyond her closest confidants, the social Two often holds the diagnosis back for a long time, worried that the intimate topic of bladder cancer might make others uncomfortable.
--- Type 3: Functioning Despite a Changed Bladder ---
SO3: How little the new urinary diversion limits her daily life is something the social Three deliberately demonstrates outwardly after the bladder removal, while practical difficulties stay hidden behind it.
SE3: Her return to her usual capacity for work is often planned by the self-preservation Three sooner after surgery than the healing process actually allows.
SX3: Her insecurity about the changed sense of her body after surgery is shown by the sexual Three more to the one important person than to the wider public, in front of whom she maintains her composure.
--- Type 4: A Place Where Shame and Illness Meet ---
SX4: The shame over a changed urinary diversion is confided directly by the sexual Four to the one person she feels bonded to, rather than treated as a taboo.
SO4: In the illness, the social Four sometimes finds a painful confirmation of her sense of being misunderstood with a condition she experiences as embarrassing, which tends to make her withdraw rather than speak up.
SE4: Her fear of surgery and changed bodily function is usually carried by the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, in a tough way with little complaint, contrary to the dramatic display otherwise typical for her type.
--- Type 5: Understanding as a Path Through Shame ---
SE5: Which forms of urinary diversion are options and how manageable they are day to day is something the self-preservation Five clarifies for herself before engaging in a conversation about a possible bladder removal.
SO5: In professionally oriented circles, the social Five prefers exchanging medical details of treatment, while her personal sense of shame around the changed bodily function usually stays unspoken.
SX5: Even a topic as initially shameful as a changed urinary diversion gets opened up by the sexual Five toward the one deep connection, rather than kept at a purely factual distance the way other Five variants tend to manage it.

Ovarian Cancer (Psychosomatics Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the ovaries that for a long time causes vague or no symptoms at all, and is therefore often discovered late.
Definition: Ovarian cancer is a malignant tumor arising from the ovaries or the neighboring fallopian tubes. Recognized risk factors include older age, hereditary predispositions such as mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, a family history of ovarian or breast cancer, never having given birth, and certain forms of endometriosis. Cervical Cancer (Psychosomatics Register · Oncology)
A malignant tumor of the cervix that in the vast majority of cases develops from infection with certain HPV types and is well detectable through screening.
Definition: Cervical cancer is a malignant tumor arising from the tissue of the cervix. The overwhelming cause is a persistent infection with certain high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV) – an extremely common viral infection that most sexually active people encounter at some point in life, and which in the vast majority of cases clears on its own without ever developing into disease. Only in a small proportion of infections does the virus persist for years, gradually promoting cell changes and eventually cancer. Other contributing factors are smoking, a weakened immune system, and the absence of regular screening. HPV vaccination significantly lowers the risk, and the Pap smear usually detects precursor changes years before they could develop into cancer – which is why cervical cancer is among the cancers best preventable through screening. Treatment ranges from surgical removal of altered tissue to removal of the uterus to radiation and chemotherapy; the prognosis is generally very good when caught early.
Typical symptoms: Unusual vaginal bleeding, for example between periods or after menopause; Bleeding after intercourse; Unusual, foul-smelling discharge; Pain in the pelvis or lower back; Pain during intercourse; Unexplained weight loss at an advanced stage
Emergency notice: Unusual bleeding, especially after intercourse or after menopause, should be checked by a doctor promptly – regular screening usually detects changes even before such symptoms appear. With known cervical cancer accompanied by heavy bleeding, severe pain, or fever, seek medical help immediately.

Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (Psychosomatics Register · Oncology)
A group of malignant diseases of the lymphatic system that can vary widely in spread, course, and aggressiveness.
Definition: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is not a single disease but a highly diverse group of malignant conditions of the lymphatic system, arising from degenerated white blood cells (lymphocytes) that can spread through lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow, and sometimes other organs. The exact cause is usually unknown; recognized risk factors include a weakened immune system (for example through immunosuppression after organ transplantation or certain infections such as HIV or Epstein-Barr virus), certain autoimmune diseases, longstanding exposure to certain chemicals, and older age. The course ranges from slow-growing forms that cause barely any impairment for years to very aggressive variants requiring rapid treatment. Depending on the subtype and stage, treatment ranges from watchful waiting to chemotherapy and antibody-based immunotherapy to stem cell transplantation; the prognosis varies considerably depending on the type of lymphoma.

Emergency notice: Painlessly swollen lymph nodes persisting for several weeks, ongoing fever, heavy night sweats, or unexplained weight loss should be checked by a doctor. With known non-Hodgkin lymphoma accompanied by high fever, marked shortness of breath, or pronounced weakness, seek medical help immediately.

Type 1 Diabetes (Psychosomatics Register · Hormones & Metabolism)
An autoimmune condition in which the body's own immune system destroys the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas – usually beginning already in childhood or adolescence, independent of lifestyle or diet.
Definition: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. Unlike type 2, type 1 has nothing to do with excess weight, diet, or lifestyle – its exact triggers are still not fully understood, though a genetic predisposition combined with environmental factors, possibly certain viral infections, is discussed. The condition typically appears already in childhood, adolescence, or young adulthood, often within a few weeks and with pronounced symptoms. Because the body can no longer produce its own insulin, those affected depend on external supply for life – through injections or an insulin pump – and must check their blood sugar several times a day. This illness is never the result of poor choices; it is a chronic underlying condition that demands a high degree of self-management from the very start, often from childhood on.
Typical symptoms: Intense thirst and very frequent urination; Rapid, unexplained weight loss; Pronounced fatigue and weakness; Ravenous hunger despite weight loss; Nausea, abdominal pain, acetone-like breath odor when blood sugar derails; Visual disturbances from fluctuating blood sugar levels
Emergency notice: Call emergency services immediately for clouded consciousness, acetone-like breath odor, severe nausea, and rapid breathing (suspected diabetic ketoacidosis). Also act immediately for severe hypoglycemia with confusion or unconsciousness.

Hyperlipidemia / Dyslipidemia (Psychosomatics Register · Hormones & Metabolism)
A fat metabolism thrown out of balance, in which cholesterol or triglycerides accumulate in the blood without those affected usually feeling anything – until the vessels take damage.
Definition: Hyperlipidemia or dyslipidemia describes a disorder of fat metabolism in which blood lipid levels – particularly LDL cholesterol and triglycerides – remain persistently elevated, while protective HDL cholesterol often stays too low. Causes can include a genetic predisposition (familial hypercholesterolemia), diet, lack of exercise, excess weight, but also other underlying conditions such as an underactive thyroid or diabetes. The insidious part: elevated blood lipid levels usually cause no noticeable symptoms for years, while deposits (plaques) quietly form in the vessel walls, considerably raising the risk of atherosclerosis, heart attack, and stroke. The diagnosis is usually made incidentally through a blood test, often only after lipid levels have already been too high, unnoticed, for years.
Typical symptoms: Usually no noticeable symptoms in the early stage; Yellowish fatty deposits on eyelids or tendons with severely elevated levels; A gray ring around the cornea (arcus lipoides) in younger people affected; Possible high blood pressure as an accompanying symptom; With severe elevation: abdominal pain from pancreatitis; Only felt late: symptoms of advanced atherosclerosis such as chest pain or shortness of breath
Emergency notice: Call emergency services immediately for sudden severe chest pain, shortness of breath, or pain radiating into the arm or jaw (suspected heart attack). Also seek immediate medical help for acute, severe abdominal pain with nausea (suspected pancreatitis caused by extremely high triglycerides).

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) (Psychosomatics Register · Other Conditions)
A benign, age-related enlargement of the prostate that affects many men as they grow older and increasingly narrows the flow of urine – not a cancer.
Definition: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a benign enlargement of the prostate that occurs in a large share of men as they age, favored by hormonal changes in the aging process, particularly a shifting ratio of testosterone to estrogens. Important for context: BPH is explicitly not a cancer and does not develop into one, even though both conditions affect the same gland and can cause similar symptoms – which is why medical evaluation remains important. The enlarged prostate surrounds the urethra and can increasingly constrict it, making urination more difficult. The course usually unfolds slowly over years, and many men unknowingly adjust to the gradual restriction before recognizing it as something that needs treatment.
Typical symptoms: Weakened or interrupted urine stream; Frequent urge to urinate, especially at night (nocturia); Sensation of incomplete bladder emptying; Difficulty starting urination; Post-void dribbling; With advanced narrowing: increased risk of urinary tract infections or urinary retention
Emergency notice: Seek prompt medical help or an emergency room for sudden inability to urinate accompanied by severe lower abdominal pain (acute urinary retention).

Cataract (Psychosomatics Register · Eyes)
A usually age-related clouding of the eye's lens, in which the world is increasingly perceived as if through a veil or a fogged-up pane of glass.
Definition: A cataract is a progressive clouding of the eye's lens, which is normally clear and directs light unimpeded onto the retina. By far the most common cause is the natural aging process, in which protein structures in the lens change and cloud over; less commonly, congenital forms, injuries, certain medications (such as cortisone), or accompanying conditions like diabetes are responsible. Unlike glaucoma, where the optic nerve is damaged by elevated pressure, a cataract affects the lens itself – the world does not narrow but grows increasingly milky, blurred, and low in contrast, as if seen through a fogged windowpane. The course usually unfolds slowly over years; surgery with lens replacement is now considered a routine procedure with very good outcomes.
Typical symptoms: Increasingly blurred, hazy vision; Diminishing contrast and color perception; Heightened glare sensitivity, especially in darkness and against bright light; Double vision in one eye; Frequent changes in eyeglass prescription; Reduced vision at dusk and while driving at night
Emergency notice: A cataract itself is not an acute emergency and usually develops over years. Still, sudden, one-sided vision loss, severe eye pain, or flashes of light with a shower of dark spots should be evaluated promptly by an ophthalmologist to rule out other, acute causes.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.

Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD) (Psychosomatics Register · Eyes)
A progressive disease of the point of sharpest vision at the center of the retina, in which the central gaze itself – on faces, letters, whatever is looked at directly – gets lost.
Definition: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) affects the macula, the point of sharpest vision at the center of the retina responsible for direct, detailed sight – such as reading, recognizing faces, or driving. A distinction is made between the more common, more slowly progressing dry form, in which visual cells in the macular region gradually die off, and the rarer but more aggressive wet form, in which abnormal, leaky blood vessels grow beneath the retina and can rapidly lead to vision loss. Unlike a cataract, which clouds the lens, or glaucoma, which narrows the outer edges of the visual field, AMD affects precisely the center of the field of view – peripheral vision usually remains intact for a long time, while a growing gap or distorted spot forms at the center. Risk factors include age, family history, smoking, and certain dietary factors.
Typical symptoms: Blurred or distorted vision at the center of the field of view; Straight lines appear wavy or bent; Increasing difficulty reading and recognizing faces; A gray or dark spot at the center of the visual field; Diminishing color vision and contrast sensitivity; Preserved, usually unremarkable peripheral vision
Emergency notice: Have sudden, rapid deterioration of central vision or newly appearing distorted lines (a possible sign of the wet form of AMD) evaluated promptly by an ophthalmologist, since early treatment can be decisive for preserving eyesight.

SE6: Warning signs such as wavy lines while reading the newspaper the self-preservation Six usually notices right away, since she is already constantly attentive to changes in her own body. This attentiveness can make AMD detectable early.
SO6: Recommendations from her ophthalmologist for regular checkups the social Six usually follows conscientiously, preferring to rely on recognized authorities over her own judgment in medical matters. This can make AMD visible early.
SX6: Distorted lines or a dark spot the sexual Six, the counter-type, brings up assertively with her ophthalmologist, rather than carrying the worry silently on her own. This directness sets her apart from the quieter brooding of the other Six variants.
--- Type 7: The Seven ---
SE7: A gray spot right where her gaze would most like to rest on new, clearly experienced impressions sits poorly with the self-preservation Seven's outlook on life. Early signs are therefore readily dismissed as temporary.
SO7: During a shared outing, the social Seven, the counter-type, mentions her own vision trouble mostly in passing, so as not to dampen the group's mood. A personal eye appointment easily slips out of view this way.
SX7: A thorough eye exam is something the sexual Seven will actually make time for, once it concerns the one person who truly matters to her, rather than pushing the topic aside. This selective seriousness sets her apart from the more restless avoidance most other Seven variants fall back on.
--- Type 8: The Eight ---
SE8: As long as she still somehow gets by, the self-preservation Eight talks down a distorted spot in her field of vision, rather than treating it as a signal to be taken seriously. This denial can leave AMD untreated for a long time.
SO8: As the go-to person for other people's problems, the social Eight still sees herself even once her own central vision is noticeably declining – admitting her own weakness barely occurs to her.
SX8: How much the distorted vision unsettles her in daily life is something the sexual Eight admits only to the one person she truly trusts. This protected space can move her toward timely treatment more readily than the sustained toughness most other Eight variants hold onto.
--- Type 9: The Nine ---
SE9: An increasingly blurred center of the visual field the self-preservation Nine often notices as a problem only late, so thoroughly does she adjust to gradual change. This habituation can leave AMD unnoticed for years, until the gap at the center becomes clearly felt.
SO9: So as not to cause a fuss, the social Nine tends to keep quiet within her group about faces and letters growing increasingly blurred to her. This quiet restraint can mean AMD is only recognized late.
SX9: It usually takes her partner noticing how much she squints while reading before the sexual Nine agrees to an eye appointment. Without this outside push, her own symptoms can stay in the background for a particularly long time.
No one at an advanced age is immune to age-related macular degeneration, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict. What shows up is simply that each of the 27 subtypes handles a blurring center of their own in its own way – some through denial, others through caring for others, quiet adaptation, or a long-overridden warning signal of their own. This is exactly where the Enneagram homeopathy of this compass begins: not at the outer symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance. When this life force – regardless of which of the 27 subtypes is affected – is brought back into balance, the symptoms can resolve holistically rather than merely being suppressed on the surface.

Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the legs no longer keep up on a path that has long since grown too narrow.
Definition: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD), colloquially known as „intermittent claudication“ or „window-shopper's disease,“ refers to a usually arteriosclerotic narrowing or blockage of the arteries in the legs (less commonly the arms). Under exertion, the muscles no longer receive enough oxygen, causing exertion-dependent pain that typically forces a stop after a short walking distance – hence the nickname: sufferers appear to pause in front of shop windows, but are actually waiting for the pain to subside. Left untreated, PAD can progress to critical ischemia with the threat of tissue loss.
Typical symptoms: Exertion-dependent, cramp-like pain in the calf, thigh, or buttock that forces a stop after a short walking distance and quickly eases at rest; Cool, pale skin on the legs or feet, weakened or absent pulses; Poorly healing wounds or ulcers on toes or feet; In advanced stages: pain at rest, including at night, that improves when the leg is dangled; Hair loss on the lower legs, brittle toenails as signs of reduced blood flow
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden, severe pain with a pale, cold, numb limb (acute arterial occlusion) or signs of dying tissue (blackening, a spreading wound that shows no sign of healing): call emergency services immediately or go to an emergency room without delay. An acute vascular occlusion is a time-critical emergency in which every hour can decide whether the limb is saved – there is no room for psychosomatic interpretation here.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
PAD strikes people quite literally where they move: in the legs, the tool we use to travel toward or away from something. Conventional medicine sees mainly arteriosclerosis, favored by smoking, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Psychosomatics often reads the forced pause the disease imposes on walking as a symbol: a path walked for years with the handbrake on, a forward motion that stood in its own way, or a movement through life that never truly ran free.
--- Type 1: The Path That Must Be Controlled ---
SE1: Wherever the self-preservation One walks, she walks according to plan – no step without purpose, no detour without a guilty conscience. This constant self-control over her own pace can continue physically: a vascular system that lets go just as little as the inner critic who judges every pause as negligence.
SO1: The social One rarely walks for herself, but in service of the good cause – from appointment to appointment, obligation to obligation, never questioning her own tempo. That the body must eventually come to a literal standstill can feel like a contradiction to a self-image that barely knows stillness.
SX1: For the sexual One, walking is often a walking toward one another – with high intensity, with the demand to meet the partner as an equal. When the body unwillingly slows the pace, it strikes a subtype whose closeness is strongly defined by shared movement and presence.
--- Type 2: The Path to Others ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two is constantly on the move for others – shopping, delivering, fetching, caring – and would rather hide a painful step than admit to it. PAD's forced walking pause hits a person who can barely fit pausing into her self-image as a pillar of support.
SO2: The social Two moves through the collective – from meeting to meeting, obligation to obligation – to stay present and needed everywhere. A walking distance that abruptly ends collides with the need to remain reachable and in motion for many.
SX2: The sexual Two walks toward the one important person, physically as much as emotionally, with full intensity. Having to stop along the way while the other keeps going touches a deep fear of being left behind – a fear that reaches far beyond the purely physical.
--- Type 3: The Path to the Goal ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three walks purposefully and efficiently, every step counted, every stretch optimized. A body that forces her to slow down or stop is quickly experienced as a disruption to her own efficiency program, not as a signal.
SO3: The social Three walks where she is seen – purposeful, visible, at a pace that signals success. A visible limp or frequent stopping contradicts the image she wants to present publicly, and is therefore gladly concealed or downplayed for as long as possible.
SX3: The sexual Three wants to appear attractive and effortless even while walking, especially in front of the one important person. A painfully limited walking distance strikes hard at the self-image of flawless allure this subtype particularly cultivates in intimate settings.
--- Type 4: The Path That Feels Different Than Dreamed ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four keeps functioning outwardly, unnoticed, even when walking becomes harder – complaining doesn't fit this counter-type's quiet endurance. The longing for a freer, lighter life stays unspoken inside.
SO4: Speaking openly about her exhaustion and pain while walking, seeking understanding, and sharing the suffering with others is the social Four's path. This expression can bring relief, but it also makes the physical limitation part of her identity as the one who suffers most visibly.
SX4: The sexual Four often experiences restricted mobility as further proof of a life that falls short of the longed-for intensity – a comparison with how things could be that makes the real walking distance feel even heavier.
--- Type 5: The Path That Rarely Went Far Anyway ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five has often already kept her radius voluntarily small for a long time to conserve energy. A physically limited walking distance fits almost seamlessly into an already reduced lifestyle – which makes it easy to overlook the warning sign.
SO5: The social Five moves observantly at the edge of events, rarely in the thick of things. Frequent stops while walking fit an already withdrawn position, which can mean the limitation goes unrecognized as a problem in its own right for a long time.
SX5: The sexual Five moves intensely, but only within the narrow radius of a few trusted people. When even that small radius is further constricted by pain while walking, it strikes a bond that is already kept selective and rare.
--- Type 6: The Path Under Permanent Alert ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six plans routes in advance, calculates risks, prepares for the worst. An illness that makes walking itself uncertain confirms and reinforces an already vigilant, cautious basic stance toward her own body.
SO6: The social Six often orients her walking to the group, to shared routes and shared routines. Falling behind because the legs no longer cooperate touches a deeper worry: losing connection to the community.
SX6: The sexual Six walks forward counterphobically and boldly, seeking challenge instead of caution. An illness that exposes her own body as suddenly vulnerable contradicts the self-chosen image of strength especially sharply.
--- Type 7: The Path That Must Not End ---
SE7: Keeping several paths and options open at once, always moving between possibilities – that is the self-preservation Seven's basic pattern. A limited walking distance feels especially cutting here, because it curtails exactly the freedom from which this subtype draws her sense of security.
SO7: The counter-type among the Sevens, the social Seven, often sets aside her own physical limits in favor of others and keeps walking even though the pain has long urged her to stop. This denial of her own signals can let the disease progress unnoticed.
SX7: The sexual Seven lives intensity and pace even in walking itself – fast, impatient, already anticipating the next experience. A body that forces a pause hits hard against an impatience that can barely tolerate standstill.
--- Type 8: The Path That May Never Show Weakness ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight proves strength partly through physical toughness and often keeps walking through pain for a long time without a word. This very silence can mean the disease is only noticed late.
SO8: The social Eight walks ahead, takes the lead, even physically – as someone who protects and carries others. Having to slow down herself is quickly experienced as an attack on her role as the group's strong head.
SX8: The sexual Eight lives physical intensity unchecked, including while walking together with her partner. An illness that physically limits this intensity is rarely accepted without a fight, and is often bluffed through for as long as possible instead.
--- Type 9: The Path No One Should Notice ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine walks her habitual routine, avoiding attention, even for her own pain. Her own complaints are often only taken seriously once walking has become practically impossible – a very literal example of self-forgetting.
SO9: The social Nine adapts her pace to the group and avoids standing out with her own complaints or holding others up. This consideration can mean pain signals while walking get downplayed for a long time.
SX9: The sexual Nine prefers to walk in step with her beloved, merging with their pace. Unable to keep up any longer, she experiences it not only physically but as a rupture of the merging that means the most to her.
No subtype is immune to PAD, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is that each of the 27 subtypes has its own particular relationship to its own forward motion – some through controlling the pace, others through withdrawal, denial of pain, or the fear of losing connection. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not with the narrowed vessel, but with the life force that has fallen out of balance, which also shows itself in one's own walking pace.

Pulmonary Embolism (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When a sudden blockage of the lung takes away breath that was already scarce.
Definition: A pulmonary embolism occurs when a blood clot (thrombus) – usually originating in the deep leg veins – travels through the bloodstream into the pulmonary arteries and blocks one or more vessels there. Depending on the size of the blockage, the clinical picture ranges from barely noticeable symptoms to acute circulatory collapse. Risk factors include prolonged immobility, surgery, pregnancy, smoking, obesity, and inherited clotting disorders.
