Typical symptoms: Sudden-onset shortness of breath, often at rest and without an obvious trigger; Sharp, breath-dependent chest pain; Rapid heartbeat, dizziness up to fainting; Coughing, in some cases with blood-streaked sputum; Often accompanied by: swelling, pain, or warmth in one leg as a sign of deep vein thrombosis; A feeling of anxiety and constriction that goes beyond mere breathlessness
Emergency notice: A pulmonary embolism is ALWAYS an acute medical emergency. In the case of sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, dizziness, fainting, or coughing blood: call emergency services immediately. This holds regardless of how mild the symptoms seem and regardless of how well the affected person still feels in the moment – a blockage can worsen dramatically within minutes. There is no room for psychosomatic interpretation here, only for immediate emergency care.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Few conditions in this compass show as vividly how something accumulated unnoticed for a long time can suddenly break loose and take the breath away: a clot that formed quietly and mostly unnoticed in a leg vein travels through the bloodstream to the lungs and, within seconds, blocks exactly what the body otherwise needs to breathe freely. Psychosomatics often reads in this an image of something held back for a long time that suddenly releases and strikes exactly where life is felt most immediately – in the breath.
--- Type 1: When Held-Back Pressure Suddenly Releases ---
SE1: The self-preservation One keeps her tension under control for a long time, disciplined, almost invisible. That something held back for so long suddenly and uncontrollably releases, as happens in an embolism, stands in sharp contrast to a life built on constant mastery.
SO1: The social One carries her tension as responsibility for the greater good, often for years without a real break. A sudden, acute event like an embolism can feel like a moment in which the body forces a pause the alert mind would never have allowed itself.
SX1: In the sexual One, tension usually discharges directly within the relationship, in words, in confrontation. An event that literally takes the breath away meets a subtype whose usual outlets are more verbal than suddenly physical.
--- Type 2: When Immobility Becomes a Danger ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two puts her own needs – including movement and rest – last for so long that eventually the body itself resorts to a final measure. Long stretches of self-neglect, especially during physical immobility, can foster a risk that goes overlooked for a long time.
SO2: The social Two barely allows herself a pause between her efforts for others – paradoxically not even the necessary movement in between, when she spends days organizing and planning for others while seated.
SX2: The sexual Two focuses all attention on the one bond and easily neglects her own physical care in the process. A sudden emergency like an embolism can, in this context, also be experienced as a painful reminder that self-care can no longer be postponed.
--- Type 3: When the Engine Stops Abruptly ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three often functions to the point of complete exhaustion, without taking real breaks – even physically, for instance after long periods of sitting or travel. A sudden vascular blockage strikes a self-image that fundamentally rates standstill as failure.
SO3: The social Three chases from one visible success to the next, often under considerable time pressure, with little regard for bodily warning signs. An acute event like an embolism forces exactly the full stop this subtype rarely allows herself.
SX3: Never wanting to appear weak or vulnerable, not even in the closest circle, leads the sexual Three to override physical signals for a correspondingly long time. A sudden, dramatic illness tears this facade open abruptly, without warning.
--- Type 4: When Pent-Up Pain Takes the Breath Away ---
SE4: Little of what happens inwardly reaches the surface with the self-preservation Four, who quietly carries on regardless. A sudden physical breakdown like an embolism can feel like a drastic, bodily version of what had long been felt inside but never given room.
SO4: The social Four speaks openly about emotional strain, which gives her a certain outlet – but bodily warning signs like leg swelling or shortness of breath are not automatically taken more seriously as a result, when the focus lies mainly on emotional expression.
SX4: The sexual Four lives intensity without compromise, even once the body has long since signaled its limits. A sudden, dramatic event fits, in a way, a way of living that rarely knows in-between tones – but it is rarely read in time as its own warning sign.
--- Type 5: When Withdrawal Stalls the Circulation ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five often reduces movement and contact to a minimum to conserve energy. Long, sedentary stretches favor circulatory stagnation, which is especially easy to overlook in this subtype given her general withdrawal.
SO5: The social Five prefers observing to actively participating, spending much time in quiet, seated distance from events. Bodily warning signs are often registered purely cognitively here, but not translated into concrete action.
SX5: The sexual Five concentrates her limited energy on the few trusted bonds and easily neglects her own everyday movement. A sudden emergency meets a person who allows bodily signals to register only late.
--- Type 6: When Fear Is Suddenly Proven Right ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six takes precautions, calculates risks – yet of all things, a sudden, barely predictable event like an embolism can disturbingly confirm her own caution and further heighten an already vigilant state of alarm.
SO6: The social Six orients herself to what the community considers safe, and often only accepts warning signs once they are confirmed from outside – say, by a doctor. A sudden emergency can plunge this subtype into especially deep insecurity.
SX6: The sexual Six meets danger counterphobically, by challenging it rather than avoiding it – bodily warning signs, too, are sometimes deliberately ignored to prove strength. An acute event disproves this strategy in a painful way.
--- Type 7: When Pace Suddenly Becomes Impossible ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven constantly keeps several options open and is rarely truly moved to rest – not even after long trips or surgeries, when movement would actually be advisable. This can favor exactly the risk in question.
SO7: Warning signs like leg swelling or sudden shortness of breath are often ignored longer than is safe by the social Seven, the counter-type among the Sevens, because her own physical needs are set aside in favor of others.
SX7: The sexual Seven lives at full speed until a sudden physical breakdown brings everything to an abrupt halt – a harsh contrast to a life that otherwise consistently avoids standstill.
--- Type 8: When Strength Delays the Emergency ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight consistently overrides bodily warning signs, as a matter of principle: showing weakness is out of the question. This very stance can cost dangerously precious time in a condition that requires quick action.
SO8: The social Eight looks after others first and puts her own health last, as long as the group still seems to need her. A sudden emergency is often only taken seriously once it can no longer be overlooked.
SX8: The sexual Eight lives intensity with full force and often overrides bodily signals even in close relationships. An acute event like an embolism abruptly and unbidden shatters this self-overestimation.
--- Type 9: When One's Own Body Finally Must Be Heard ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine often overrides her own complaints out of habit, not courage – her own body is rarely truly listened to. An acute emergency forces exactly the self-attention this subtype otherwise finds hardest.
SO9: The social Nine adapts to the group's rhythm and reports her own complaints only late, so as not to burden anyone. A sudden emergency interrupts this restraint involuntarily, but unmistakably.
SX9: The sexual Nine is so entirely oriented toward her beloved that her own bodily signals easily fade into the background. An acute event abruptly pulls attention back to her own body, which until then had barely had a voice of its own.
No subtype is immune to a pulmonary embolism, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is that each of the 27 subtypes deals in its own way with immobility, pent-up tension, and overridden bodily signals. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not with the acute vascular blockage itself, but with the life force that has fallen out of balance, which already shows itself long before the emergency.

Aortic Aneurysm (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the body's largest artery gives way under years of pressure, quietly and without warning.
Definition: An aortic aneurysm is a pathological, usually arteriosclerotic bulging of the main artery (aorta), most often in the abdomen (abdominal aortic aneurysm), less commonly in the chest (thoracic aneurysm). High blood pressure, smoking, genetic predisposition, or inflammatory processes cause the vessel wall to lose elasticity and slowly expand over years. As long as the aneurysm does not rupture, it usually causes no symptoms at all and is often discovered by chance during an examination.
Typical symptoms: Usually no symptoms for years – the aneurysm grows silently; With larger aneurysms, occasional diffuse back or abdominal pain, a pulsating sensation in the abdomen; When pressing on surrounding structures: a feeling of fullness, difficulty swallowing (with thoracic aneurysm), hoarseness; Sudden, extremely severe, devastating pain in the abdomen, back, or chest as a sign of an impending or actual rupture; In the event of rupture: circulatory collapse, paleness, loss of consciousness
Emergency notice: A ruptured aneurysm is an acutely life-threatening emergency. In the case of sudden, extremely severe abdominal, back, or chest pain, especially combined with circulatory collapse, paleness, or clouded consciousness: call emergency services immediately. An untreated ruptured aortic aneurysm leads to death within a very short time – every minute counts, and there is no room here for psychosomatic interpretation, only for immediate emergency care.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Hardly any vessel carries as much pressure as the aorta, the body's largest artery, through which the entire blood volume is pressed with every heartbeat. An aneurysm forms where this wall can no longer withstand that pressure over the years and slowly, silently expands – until it gives way, often without any warning. Psychosomatics often reads in this the image of a baseline tension carried for years, barely visible from the outside, yet stretching one's own substance from within until the limit of what can be borne is eventually reached.
--- Type 1: The Wall That Must Never Give Way ---
SE1: The self-preservation One maintains her composure for decades, outwardly disciplined, inwardly under constant pressure. A vessel that gives way exactly where the pressure is greatest can be read as the bodily echo of a life that tolerates no visible weakening.
SO1: The social One carries the burden of responsibility for the greater good for years, never openly naming this pressure. The silent, gradual expansion of an aneurysm resembles the slow yielding of a wall that has carried too much for too long.
SX1: Direct confrontation rather than quiet yielding marks the sexual One – here the silent, slow stretching of the wall is absent, but the intense relational dynamic places its own episodic pressure load on the vascular system.
--- Type 2: The Wall That Carries for Others ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two carries the practical burden for others for decades, never carried herself in return. This quiet, never-demanded overload can be mirrored in a vessel that likewise gives way unnoticed, because no one is watching.
SO2: The social Two spreads her strength across many shoulders at once, often overextending herself without even realizing it. The creeping expansion of an aneurysm fits an overload that accumulates unnoticed through many small obligations.
SX2: The sexual Two ties her entire strength to a single, intense relationship. When this bond becomes unstable, an emotional pressure load arises that is episodic but severe, and can act on an already strained vascular system.
--- Type 3: The Wall That Must Always Keep Functioning ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three functions at full throttle for years, never allowing herself real recovery. A vessel that slowly gives way under constant pressure fits a body that was never officially permitted a break.
SO3: The social Three lives under the constant pressure of visible comparison, an inner race with no finish line. This constant, self-generated pressure can, over decades, also leave its mark on the walls of her own vessels.
SX3: The sexual Three maintains peak performance even in private, never admitting exhaustion. The expansion of an aneurysm, much like that exhaustion, proceeds unseen behind a flawless facade for a long time.
--- Type 4: The Wall That Holds the Unspoken Pain ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four carries deep, never-spoken longing within her for decades while functioning outwardly. A slowly growing, long-unnoticed bulge fits a pain that stays just as long beneath the surface.
SO4: The social Four carries her pain outward and finds in this a certain outlet that at least partly counters the inner pressure – unlike quieter suffering, which accumulates unchecked.
SX4: Recurring highs and lows mark the sexual Four's intense emotional relational dynamic. These episodic peaks of strain place a different kind of demand on the vascular system than a steady, silent, constant tension.
--- Type 5: The Wall No One Checks ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five withdraws and avoids even doctor's visits that might feel intrusive. An aneurysm, which usually stays undetected without a targeted examination, fits a subtype who is reluctant to relinquish control over her own body.
SO5: The social Five observes the world from a certain distance and easily neglects her own preventive care as a result. An aneurysm's silent, symptomless nature makes it especially easy to overlook for years.
SX5: The sexual Five confides in only very few people – health concerns, too, often go unspoken. This reticence can mean a growing aneurysm goes unnoticed for a long time by anyone who might ask questions.
--- Type 6: The Wall That Ruptures in a Real Emergency ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six takes precautions and tends to get checked regularly, driven by the worry of missing something. This vigilance can genuinely help with early detection of an aneurysm – though the underlying constant tension remains a risk factor regardless.
SO6: The social Six follows what authorities and doctors recommend, and tends to attend preventive checkups mostly when institutionally prescribed. Without that connection, an aneurysm can easily go undetected.
SX6: The sexual Six meets fear counterphobically and sometimes deliberately avoids preventive checkups, so as not to have to admit anything to herself. This denial can be especially risky with a long-symptomless condition like an aneurysm.
--- Type 7: The Wall That Knows No Pause ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven prefers staying occupied with options over uncomfortable checkup appointments. A condition that only becomes noticeable at the abrupt moment of rupture fits, tragically well, a way of living that avoids standstill and pause.
SO7: Checkup appointments for herself regularly fall by the wayside for the social Seven, the counter-type among the Sevens, because others' needs always seem more urgent. An aneurysm growing unnoticed for years fits this chronically denied neediness.
SX7: Without a brake, the sexual Seven lives intensity, often paired with elevated nicotine or alcohol consumption – both recognized risk factors for the vessel wall, compounding an already restless way of life.
--- Type 8: The Wall That Admits No Weakness ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight consistently ignores bodily warning signs, as a matter of principle. A long-undetected, growing bulge fits a subtype who experiences preventive checkups as unnecessary condescension.
SO8: The social Eight looks after everyone but herself and notoriously postpones her own preventive care. The sudden emergency of a ruptured aneurysm meets a person who has long refused to allow her own vulnerability.
SX8: Warning signals get overridden even in close relationships by the sexual Eight, whose unchecked physical intensity leaves little room for a partner's caution to land. This self-overestimation can turn dangerous with a silent condition like an aneurysm.
--- Type 9: The Wall No One Should Notice ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine avoids uncomfortable doctor's appointments and her own health concerns out of habit. An aneurysm that causes no symptoms for years can go especially unnoticed in this subtype.
SO9: The social Nine subordinates her own health worries to peace within the group and rarely speaks up about complaints on her own. This reticence makes it harder to detect a silent, symptomless aneurysm in time.
SX9: The sexual Nine directs her entire attention to her beloved and easily neglects her own preventive care as a result. Her own body stays unheard until an acute event finally becomes impossible to ignore.
No subtype is immune to an aortic aneurysm, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is that each of the 27 subtypes deals in its own way with long-term, often invisible pressure and with its own preventive care. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not with the already-stretched vessel wall, but with the life force that has fallen out of balance, carrying that pressure unnoticed for years.

Cardiomyopathy (Psychosomatics Register · Cardiovascular System)
When the heart muscle itself loses its shape, independent of the vessels that supply it.
Definition: Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the heart muscle itself that are not primarily caused by narrowed coronary arteries or high blood pressure. Distinctions include dilated cardiomyopathy (the heart muscle weakens and the chambers widen, pumping power declines), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (the heart muscle thickens pathologically, often genetically caused), and so-called stress cardiomyopathy („broken heart syndrome,“ Takotsubo syndrome), which typically occurs acutely after extreme emotional or physical strain and shows the link between emotional shock and heart function especially directly.
Typical symptoms: Increasing shortness of breath, initially under exertion, later also at rest; Rapid exhaustion, reduced physical capacity; Heart rhythm disturbances, palpitations, racing heart; Fluid retention (edema) in the legs or abdomen as a sign of heart failure; In stress cardiomyopathy: sudden, heart-attack-like chest pain immediately after severe emotional shock, without an actual vascular blockage; Dizziness, in severe cases fainting
Emergency notice: In the case of sudden chest pain, acute shortness of breath, fainting, or suspected acute heart failure (e.g. after severe emotional strain): call emergency services immediately, since it is clinically nearly impossible to distinguish a true vascular blockage from an acute cardiomyopathy. With a known cardiomyopathy and sudden deterioration (severe shortness of breath, marked weight gain from fluid retention, clouded consciousness): also seek emergency medical care without delay.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Stress cardiomyopathy, aptly nicknamed „broken heart syndrome,“ is one of the few cardiac diagnoses in which the link between emotional shock and heart function is medically recognized directly: after the death of a loved one, a breakup, or a shock event, the left heart chamber can acutely deform in a way that resembles, on imaging, a traditional Japanese octopus trap (takotsubo). The other cardiomyopathies, too, affect the heart muscle itself, not merely its blood supply – psychosomatics often reads in this the question of how much emotional shock, sustained strain, or suppressed grief a heart muscle can carry over time before its very shape begins to change.
--- Type 1: When Inner Pressure Reshapes the Form ---
SE1: The self-preservation One maintains form and control at any cost, down to the last muscle. That of all things the heart muscle itself changes pathologically, even while everything outwardly stays disciplined, can be read as the bodily irony of a life that controlled almost everything except its own heartbeat.
SO1: Making the world more just is a burden the social One shoulders for years, never listening to her own exhaustion in the process. A slowly developing heart muscle weakness fits an engine that ran for others for decades without ever being serviced itself.
SX1: For the sexual One, a sudden, severe relational shock – a breakup, a betrayal – can be exactly the acute emotional jolt described as a trigger for stress cardiomyopathy: the heart here reacts directly to what breaks close by.
--- Type 2: When the Heart Beats for Others Until It Gives Way Itself ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two practically cares for others for decades, never cared for herself in return. A creeping weakening of the heart muscle fits an organ that has given for a long time without ever getting anything back.
SO2: The social Two spreads her care across many people at once, often overextending herself unnoticed. The quiet overload of a heart that wants to be there for too many at once can, over time, show up as declining pumping capacity.
SX2: A single relationship carries the sexual Two's entire self-worth – should it break, the emotional collapse is especially severe. Exactly such an acute, heart-wrenching event is considered a classic trigger of stress cardiomyopathy.
--- Type 3: When Performance Overtaxes the Heart Muscle ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three drives her body to the limit for years, often also athletically, without real recovery phases. An overburdened heart muscle that changes pathologically can express a system that never officially got a break.
SO3: The social Three lives under constant comparison pressure – a state cardiologically linked to increased strain on the heart muscle. Unlike a classic vascular blockage, what shows up here tends to be a creeping fatigue of the muscle itself.
SX3: The sexual Three rarely lets her flawless self-image collapse in public – but should it happen, say through a sudden relational failure, the emotional force of that collapse can trigger exactly the acute heart reaction described as stress cardiomyopathy.
--- Type 4: When Grief Settles Into the Muscle ---
SE4: Deep, never-spoken grief stays locked inside the self-preservation Four for years while she keeps functioning outwardly. A creeping change in the heart muscle fits a pain that finds expression inward rather than outward.
SO4: The social Four expresses grief openly and finds in this a certain outlet that at least partly counters the purely physical strain. Still, the risk of acute stress cardiomyopathy remains real, especially after severe loss.
SX4: The sexual Four lives heartbreak with an intensity all its own – a broken heart is, for this subtype, almost literal, and is considered psycho-cardiologically one of the most classic triggers of stress cardiomyopathy.
--- Type 5: When Withdrawal Undersupplies the Heart Muscle ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five reduces contact and movement alike to conserve energy. A heart muscle that is rarely challenged and rarely emotionally touched can, over the long run, also lose adaptability.
SO5: The social Five maintains emotional distance even where she is physically present. This chronic inner remoteness makes it harder to notice early warning signs of a developing heart muscle weakness at all.
SX5: The sexual Five bonds intensely, but only to very few people – the loss of such a rare, deep bond can trigger an emotional shock whose force comes close to that of a stress cardiomyopathy, since so little else absorbs the loss.
--- Type 6: When Constant Alarm Wears Down the Heart Muscle ---
SE6: Constant caution and inner alertness mark the self-preservation Six's everyday life. Chronically elevated stress hormone levels are a plausible mechanism for a gradual wearing down of the heart muscle, even without a single, concrete shock event.
SO6: The social Six worries above all about preserving the community her own security depends on. A sudden break in that belonging – say, losing an important group or institution – can trigger an acute emotional shock.
SX6: The sexual Six seeks proof of herself in deliberately sought confrontation, which generates episodic but intense peaks of strain. A sudden, unexpected defeat in such a self-sought battle can act as an acute emotional shock.
--- Type 7: When Distraction Masks Grief Until It Breaks Through ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven keeps real feeling at bay with an endless stream of new options. Should this evasion ever collapse – say through an event that cannot be planned away – the pent-up emotional force can surface especially abruptly.
SO7: Exhaustion is denied for a long time by the social Seven, the counter-type among the Sevens, as long as someone else still seems to need her strength. Should this facade suddenly collapse, it can, like with other chronically denying subtypes, show up as an acute heart reaction.
SX7: The sexual Seven lives intensity unchecked, often accompanied by elevated consumption of nicotine, alcohol, or other taxing indulgences – recognized risk factors that can act on the heart muscle in addition to emotional volatility.
--- Type 8: When Strength Itself Leads to the Break ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight rarely lets weakness or vulnerability show, even amid deep loss. This very denial can mean an emotional shock hits the body suddenly and hard, because it never found a regular outlet.
SO8: The social Eight protects and carries others, even while her own heart is already overburdened. Should this protective role suddenly fall away – say through the loss of someone she has protected – the emotional force can be especially severe.
SX8: Total devotion marks the sexual Eight's one relationship – a sudden end to that bond hits accordingly with full force, without the cushioning a broader emotional network could offer.
--- Type 9: When One's Own Heart Finally Gets a Say ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine represses her own emotional pain in favor of comfort and routine, often for decades. A heart muscle that slowly changes can be read as the bodily echo of a heart that was never truly heard.
SO9: The social Nine consistently subordinates her own feelings to group harmony. A sudden rupture within the community that cannot be harmonized away can trigger an emotional shock this subtype otherwise hardly ever allows.
SX9: So completely does the sexual Nine merge with her beloved that their loss feels like a loss of her own identity – psycho-cardiologically one of the most vivid conceivable triggers of stress cardiomyopathy.
No subtype is immune to cardiomyopathy, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is that the heart muscle itself – independent of its vessels – negotiates sustained strain, sudden loss, or never-expressed grief in its own way for each of the 27 subtypes. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not with the altered muscle tissue, but with the life force that has fallen out of balance, which gives this muscle its shape.

Gastritis (Psychosomatics Register · Digestive System)
When the stomach lining reacts, inflamed, to what the stomach can no longer digest.
Definition: Gastritis is an inflammation of the stomach lining that can be acute (often caused by alcohol, medications such as pain relievers, stress, or an infection) or chronic. The most common cause of chronic gastritis is infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori; autoimmune processes or chronic irritation from bile reflux play a role less often. Left untreated, chronic gastritis can raise the risk of stomach ulcers and, in rare cases, stomach cancer.
Typical symptoms: A feeling of pressure or fullness in the upper abdomen, often after eating; Nausea, occasional vomiting; Burning or gnawing pain in the upper abdomen; Loss of appetite, feeling full prematurely; Belching, heartburn; In acute gastritis with a tendency to bleed: vomiting blood or black-colored stool (warning sign)
Emergency notice: In the case of vomiting blood, black, tarry stool, sudden severe abdominal pain, or circulatory weakness: seek emergency medical care immediately or call emergency services, as this can indicate acute stomach bleeding. There is no room for psychosomatic interpretation here, only for immediate medical evaluation.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
In many body-image traditions, the stomach is the place where we quite literally digest what life serves us – impressions, conflicts, expectations that are not always easy to stomach. Conventional medicine sees gastritis mainly as a combination of irritants such as Helicobacter pylori, medications, or stress, which affect stomach acid production and the blood supply to the lining. Traditional Chinese Medicine assigns the stomach to the Earth element and often links stomach complaints to rumination and excessive overthinking. Psychosomatics often reads in the inflamed lining an image of something that cannot, or must not, be digested right now – anger, a demand, a pace that leaves the stomach literally sour.
--- Type 1: What the Stomach Refuses to Swallow ---
SE1: The self-preservation One regularly swallows her anger instead of voicing it – quite literally: criticism, disappointment, and rage are disciplined into suppression and land in the stomach instead, which can respond to this sustained strain with heightened irritability.
SO1: The social One digests not only her own anger but, it can feel, the injustices of the entire world – a workload that rarely lets the stomach settle, because the inner reform work never really clocks off.
SX1: The sexual One carries her anger directly into the relationship, where it is at least partly voiced – yet the demand for perfection in closeness remains a source of recurring tension that can also make itself felt in the stomach.
--- Type 2: What Is Given on an Empty Stomach ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two often looks after others before she has eaten herself – meals get skipped or gulped down hastily between tasks. This irregularity alone can irritate the stomach lining, quite apart from any emotional component.
SO2: The social Two is constantly on call for many people at once and often eats on the side, under time pressure, mind already on the next obligation – a pattern that leaves the stomach little chance for real rest.
SX2: The sexual Two lives in constant worry about the one important bond, a tension that can easily show up as loss of appetite or a queasy, nervous stomach, especially in phases of insecurity.
--- Type 3: What Gets Bolted Down Quickly ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three often eats on the go, functionally, without a real pause – efficiency applies to meals too. This haste while eating is one of the most direct burdens on an already irritated stomach lining.
SO3: Even business meals and appointments for the social Three revolve around visible success rather than actual enjoyment, serving representation instead – a constant pressure that barely pauses even at the table.
SX3: Even a shared meal is a stage for the sexual Three, who prefers to suppress her own discomfort rather than jeopardize the flawless impression she wants to leave. The stomach rarely gets the attention it would actually need.
--- Type 4: What the Stomach Feels Along With ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four often carries unspoken grief quietly within her while functioning outwardly – a stomach that sits on years of never-expressed pain can answer with chronic irritation.
SO4: Grief finds an open outlet with the social Four, who talks about what hurts – stomach complaints here tend to appear episodically after emotional highs rather than as a constant, silent irritation.
SX4: The sexual Four lives intense emotional swings within the relationship, with phases of fierce excitement or despair that can immediately register in a sensitive stomach.
--- Type 5: What Is Held Back Until It Burns ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five often eats irregularly, minimally, sometimes forgetting meals entirely while absorbed in a subject. This irregularity can irritate the stomach lining just as much as emotional tension.
SO5: The social Five keeps inner distance even while eating together and rarely shares what is really on her mind. This chronic inner reticence is a quiet form of tension that can settle in the stomach.
SX5: The sexual Five opens up intensely to only very few people – worries that cannot be shared, because the circle of trust is so small, often stay lodged in her own stomach.
--- Type 6: What the Alert Stomach Constantly Checks ---
SE6: Constant caution defines the self-preservation Six's daily life, and this vigilance extends into the stomach: an organ that, through the vegetative nervous connection, reacts especially sensitively to chronic tension.
SO6: The social Six worries about the survival of the community her security depends on – a diffuse, often unnamed worry that can easily express itself as a nervous, irritated stomach.
SX6: Deliberate provocation and risk-taking are the sexual Six's way of counterphobically meeting fear – the resulting episodic adrenaline surges can irritate the stomach briefly but distinctly.
--- Type 7: What Finds No Peace Between Bites ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven likes to eat a varied diet, switching quickly between options, often with little regard for regularity – a pattern that can irritate the stomach lining over time.
SO7: Regular, calm meals for herself rarely rank as a priority for the social Seven, the counter-type among the Sevens, as long as someone else still seems to need something from her – a neglect that can lead to unnoticed chronic irritation.
SX7: The sexual Seven lives enjoyment intensely and without limits, often paired with elevated consumption of alcohol or hot, intense foods – both recognized irritants for the stomach lining.
--- Type 8: What Gets Swallowed Down With Full Force ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight often eats fast and hard, with little regard for signals of fullness or discomfort – strength here also means not taking her own stomach seriously.
SO8: The social Eight carries responsibility for others even at the table and sets aside her own complaints as long as the group still seems to need her – a stomach that goes unnoticed for a long time.
SX8: The sexual Eight lives intensity unchecked, including in eating and drinking within the relationship – recurring excess followed by equally intense periods of restraint strain the stomach lining in an irregular, forceful rhythm.
--- Type 9: What the Stomach Swallows for Others ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine often eats out of habit and comfort, without really listening to her own stomach – a very literal example of a self-forgetting that extends all the way into digestion.
SO9: At the table, too, the social Nine falls in with the group's rhythm and wishes and rarely voices her own needs – an adaptation that regularly overrides her own stomach.
SX9: The sexual Nine often adopts her beloved's eating habits, merging here too with their preferences instead of listening to her own signals – her own stomach easily goes unheard in the process.
No subtype is immune to gastritis, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is that each of the 27 subtypes negotiates, in its own way, what it literally cannot digest – anger, pace, irregular self-attention, or held-back grief. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not with the irritated lining itself, but with the life force that has fallen out of balance, which also shows itself in the stomach.

Pulmonary Fibrosis (Psychosomatics Register · Respiratory System & Lungs)
When lung tissue scars over the years and the space to breathe slowly narrows.
Definition: Pulmonary fibrosis refers to a progressive, usually irreversible scarring (fibrosis) of lung tissue, which makes the lungs increasingly stiff and impairs gas exchange. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, the most common form, the exact cause remains unknown; but it can also be triggered by autoimmune diseases, long-term exposure to dust or mold, certain medications, or chronic reflux. The disease usually progresses gradually over years, with steadily declining lung function.
Typical symptoms: Increasing shortness of breath, initially under exertion, over time also at rest; Dry, persistent irritant cough without sputum; Rapid exhaustion, declining physical capacity; Unintended weight loss in advanced stages; Clubbed fingers (club-shaped thickening of the fingertips) as a late sign of chronic oxygen deficiency; Bluish discoloration of the lips or fingertips in advanced disease
Emergency notice: In the case of suddenly worsening, severe shortness of breath, bluish discoloration of the lips or fingertips, or an acute deterioration in known pulmonary fibrosis: seek emergency medical care immediately or call emergency services, as this can indicate an acute exacerbation. There is no room for psychosomatic interpretation here, only for immediate medical evaluation.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
The lungs are the organ through which we exchange with the world most directly – every breath a taking in and a letting go. When the tissue scars, exactly this exchange becomes increasingly restricted: the lungs grow stiffer, the space for air narrower, without the process being reversible. Traditional Chinese Medicine traditionally links the lungs with grief and letting go. Psychosomatics often reads in the progressing scarring an image of a living space narrowed over years, of grief that could never fully release, or of an exchange with the world that has grown increasingly rigid.
--- Type 1: The Shrinking Space of Control ---
SE1: The self-preservation One often narrows her own living space herself, out of fear of mistakes and disorder. Lung tissue that stiffens over the years can be read as the bodily echo of a life that allows itself little breadth.
SO1: The social One never quite feels she can breathe freely, because there is always still something in the world to set right. This missing inner breadth, the never-reached feeling of having done enough, can eventually leave its mark physically as constriction.
SX1: The sexual One lives closeness with high intensity and little room for laxity – a tight, demanding relational space that leaves little emotional breadth to truly breathe.
--- Type 2: The Space Kept Free for Others ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two rarely allows herself space for her own needs, often for decades. A breathing space that slowly narrows fits a life that has granted itself little room to breathe freely.
SO2: The social Two spreads her attention across many people at once and rarely finds time for deep, conscious, restful breathing. This subtype's quiet overload can also show up as chronic inner constriction.
SX2: The sexual Two binds herself tightly to a single relationship, holding much room open for the other but claiming little for herself – a pattern that can settle in as emotional constriction.
--- Type 3: The Space That Knows No Breather ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three runs at full operation without planning in real recovery periods. Lung tissue that rarely gets to rest over the years can mirror this permanent state of busyness in the body.
SO3: The social Three rarely finds a moment to truly breathe out without already thinking of the next visible achievement – the constant pressure of comparison leaves little room for a breather.
SX3: Constant top performance, even in the closest circle, without ever admitting exhaustion, marks the sexual Three – a tension that can, in the long run, also affect her own breathing.
--- Type 4: The Space Narrowed by Grief ---
SE4: Functioning outward while an unspoken sorrow sits inside her for years is the self-preservation Four's quiet specialty. Traditional Chinese Medicine traditionally links the lungs to exactly this feeling – grief that finds no expression.
SO4: Speaking her grief out loud gives the social Four a certain outlet that counters pure restraint – yet lasting, deep sadness remains a theme that can accompany this subtype for years.
SX4: Longing and loss run through the sexual Four with great force, often in constant comparison with what is missing. This sustained emotional burden touches exactly the element the lungs are assigned in many traditions.
--- Type 5: The Space That Shrinks Itself Voluntarily ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five often voluntarily reduces her living space and her contacts to conserve energy. A narrowing breathing space fits, disturbingly well, a life that has already kept itself small for a long time.
SO5: Physically present but rarely truly open, the social Five maintains an inner distance that others can sense but not cross. This chronic inner reticence can settle in as a kind of symbolic constriction that leaves her own breath little breadth.
SX5: The sexual Five opens up intensely, but only to very few people, otherwise guarding radical distance. The narrowly bounded space of real closeness can be read as an image for an equally narrow breathing space.
--- Type 6: The Space Constantly Scanned for Threat ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six lives in ongoing vigilance toward possible dangers. This chronic tension can also express itself as shallow, never fully released breathing, which grants the lung tissue little real relaxation over the years.
SO6: The social Six worries constantly about the survival of the community her security depends on – a diffuse ongoing worry that can settle in as a feeling of never being able to breathe quite freely.
SX6: The sexual Six meets fear counterphobically, through deliberate confrontation and risk-taking – episodic peaks of strain that can, briefly but distinctly, also affect her breathing.
--- Type 7: The Space That Must Never Grow Narrow ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven keeps several paths open so as never to feel confined. A disease that literally narrows her own breathing space hits this subtype especially hard, because it threatens exactly the breadth from which she draws her security.
SO7: The social Seven, counter-type among the Sevens, often sets aside her own need for breadth and lightness in favor of others – a chronic self-restriction that works in the background.
SX7: Elevated nicotine consumption often accompanies the sexual Seven's unchecked intensity – a recognized risk factor for lung tissue, compounding an already restless way of life.
--- Type 8: The Space That Must Never Show Weakness ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight overrides shortness of breath and other bodily warning signs for a long time, as a matter of principle. A creeping scarring of lung tissue can thus progress unnoticed for years, until it can no longer be bluffed away.
SO8: The social Eight puts her own health last, as long as the group still seems to need her. Increasing shortness of breath is often only taken seriously once it visibly limits her own protective role for others.
SX8: The sexual Eight lives intensity unchecked and overrides bodily signals, even in close relationships. Chronic shortness of breath especially directly disrupts a self-image of strength here, because it becomes constantly visible in everyday life.
--- Type 9: The Space No One Should Notice ---
SE9: Out of pure habit, the self-preservation Nine overrides her own complaints, and increasing shortness of breath is correspondingly reported late. A slowly narrowing breathing space fits a life that rarely actively listens to its own body.
SO9: Group harmony outranks her own complaints for the social Nine, who is reluctant to speak up on her own about increasing shortness of breath, so as not to worry anyone.
SX9: The sexual Nine directs her attention almost entirely to her beloved and easily overlooks her own slowly changing breath sounds and declining stamina as a result.
No subtype is immune to pulmonary fibrosis, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is that each of the 27 subtypes deals in its own way with its own living space, with grief, and with its exchange with the world. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not with the scarred tissue itself, but with the life force that has fallen out of balance, which also shows itself in one's own breathing space.

Hepatitis B (Chronic) (Psychosomatics Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A liver inflammation that doesn't heal but becomes a permanent companion – raising the question of who to tell and who not to.
Definition: Chronic hepatitis B is an inflammation of the liver, persisting for at least six months, caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which can be transmitted through blood, sexual contact, or from mother to child. In a small proportion of those infected – especially when infection occurs in adulthood – the infection does not fully resolve, and the virus remains permanently detectable in the liver. Left untreated, chronic hepatitis B can lead over years to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, or, in rare cases, liver cancer. Modern antiviral medications, however, can reliably suppress viral replication in most affected people and keep the disease course stable for decades – chronic hepatitis B is thus, for the great majority of those affected, a well-manageable long-term condition today, not an automatic precursor to liver failure. How an infection was acquired says nothing about the character of the person affected.
Typical symptoms: Often no or only nonspecific symptoms for years (fatigue, mild discomfort in the upper right abdomen); Occasional yellowing of skin and eyes during acute flares; Elevated liver enzymes as a common incidental finding on routine tests; In late stages, signs of liver cirrhosis (fluid retention, bleeding tendency); Psychological strain from the diagnosis, disclosure questions, and uncertainty about the future
Emergency notice: See a doctor immediately for severe jaundice, confusion, bleeding, or severe abdominal pain – these can indicate acute liver decompensation.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
How a chronic hepatitis B infection was acquired plays no role in this psychosomatic reflection and carries no moral judgment whatsoever – what matters here is exclusively how a person handles the diagnosis itself: the decision of who to tell and who not to, the question of treatment adherence over the years, and the navigation of closeness and intimacy once a permanent infection has become part of one's own life. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle disclosure, treatment discipline, and their own vulnerability toward others.
--- Type 1: The One ---
SE1: The self-preservation One takes her antiviral medication with great reliability at exactly the same times each day, which gives her inner order amid a diagnosis she never chose. What often proves harder is deciding whether to tell anyone in her closest circle at all.
SO1: What she morally owes is something the social One frequently thinks through carefully with a transmissible infection – to whom does a duty of disclosure apply, and to whom not. This inner rulebook can bring relief, but can also tip into excessively harsh self-judgment where none is warranted.
SX1: Within the one important relationship, the sexual One searches for the right moment to disclose, careful not to endanger the bond by speaking too soon or too late. This precise weighing can occupy her more than the medical side of the diagnosis itself.
--- Type 2: The Two ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two often wants to protect her family from every conceivable risk of transmission, even where the actual transmission routes don't call for it. This excessive caution can stem more from concern for others than from actual risk.
SO2: Whom to tell about the diagnosis, within her wide circle of acquaintances, is something the social Two chooses very carefully, fearing she might be seen as a source of infection rather than as the helpful person she wants to be. This selective silence can isolate her more than the illness itself would.
SX2: The sexual Two usually opens up first and in full detail to the one person she feels especially close to, before she even considers telling anyone else. This early openness within the core relationship can significantly ease the burden of secrecy.
--- Type 3: The Three ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three handles her doctor's appointments and lab checks efficiently and with discipline, like just another task in her well-organized day. About the diagnosis itself, she prefers to say as little as possible.
SO3: The social Three doesn't want her flawless public image jeopardized by the diagnosis, so she often keeps chronic hepatitis B entirely quiet for years, even from close colleagues. Maintaining this facade costs her a great deal of inner energy.
SX3: The sexual Three usually tells the one person for whom she unfolds her charm about the diagnosis only once the relationship already seems solid enough to bear it. This calculated delay differs from the ongoing concealment of the other Three variants.
--- Type 4: The Four ---
SE4: Tenaciously and without much fuss, the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, usually carries her diagnosis, while quietly it deepens her sense of constantly having to fight against something in daily life.
SO4: The social Four may place a chronic hepatitis B diagnosis within her life story as further proof that she is different from others and singled out for especially hard trials. Fitting it into this larger narrative of suffering can distract from actual treatment adherence.
SX4: Within the one deep relationship, the sexual Four often reveals the diagnosis with great emotional intensity, carrying the hope of being fully understood. If that openness is met in kind, it can noticeably lighten the burden of secrecy.
--- Type 5: The Five ---
SE5: Every available piece of medical knowledge on viral course, treatment options, and prognosis, the self-preservation Five thoroughly gathers to retain a sense of control over her situation. This knowledge can be reassuring, but can also distract from emotional processing.
SO5: In relevant forums or professional circles, the social Five gladly exchanges views with other affected people, without revealing herself within her immediate surroundings. This abstract exchange can yield insight, but it doesn't replace the personal closeness that is sometimes missing.
SX5: Gathering expert knowledge about the diagnosis gives the sexual Five a sense of control she otherwise rarely feels – the fear underneath it, though, she shows almost no one except the one person she truly trusts.
--- Type 6: The Six ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six plans her medication and regular checkups with great care, at least to have reliable certainty here. Still, worry about a decline despite treatment adherence can continue to accompany her.
SO6: Her treatment team's recommendations serve as a precise compass for the social Six, who also seeks additional support in self-help groups. Clear, authoritative statements about her prognosis can noticeably ease her uncertainty.
SX6: A strikingly proactive approach is how the sexual Six, the counter-type, meets the diagnosis – she brings the topic up actively rather than hiding it, demonstrating her capacity to act through this combative stance.
--- Type 7: The Seven ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven doesn't want a permanent diagnosis to take away her accustomed lightness around physical matters, and gladly postpones dealing with it. Regular checkup appointments can easily slip her mind as a result.
SO7: The social Seven, the counter-type, typically leaves herself hardly any room for her own burden, continuing instead to devote herself to others. Keeping the diagnosis in the background rather than seriously addressing it can harm her over time.
SX7: The sexual Seven concentrates her openness about the diagnosis on the one especially meaningful relationship, rather than spreading it thinly across many contacts. This focused approach differs from the distraction strategy of the other Seven variants.
--- Type 8: The Eight ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight decides for herself when, to whom, and how she tells people about the diagnosis, and won't let this control over her own story be taken from her. This self-determination can give her a sense of security where others feel at the mercy of events.
SO8: The social Eight wants to show her strength within the group as unbroken, even with this diagnosis – admitting vulnerability contradicts her self-image as protector. Hiding it costs her more energy than is visible from outside.
SX8: Control over her own body and the prognosis is what the sexual Eight normally clings to as her anchor – how much this diagnosis actually shakes her, she reveals at most to the one person whose loyalty she has tested over years.
--- Type 9: The Nine ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine wants her familiar daily routine disturbed as little as possible by the diagnosis, which can make treatment appointments easy to lose track of. An outside nudge can help her actively bring her own health back into focus.
SO9: So as not to disturb the harmony around her, the social Nine often keeps her diagnosis quiet for a long time, out of concern that others might feel uncomfortable or distant. Setting her own situation aside like this can cost her badly needed support.
SX9: The sexual Nine, disclosing the diagnosis, tends to orient herself more by her partner's reaction than by her own processing of it. If the partner reacts calmly, she too can find it easier to face her own situation with equanimity.
Chronic hepatitis B says nothing about a person's character or way of life, regardless of how it was acquired. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes handles disclosure, treatment adherence, and their own vulnerability toward others differently – some through strict self-control, others through selective trust or setting their own situation aside. This knowledge does not replace antiviral treatment, but can help, alongside it, to understand why people with the same diagnosis cope so differently.

Hepatitis C (Chronic) (Psychosomatics Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A liver infection that is usually curable today – but the path to diagnosis is often a long one of not knowing.
Definition: Chronic hepatitis C is an inflammation of the liver, persisting for at least six months, caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV), which is transmitted mainly through blood contact – for instance through shared needles, contaminated medical instruments in the past, or, more rarely, sexual contact. Unlike hepatitis B, the infection resolves on its own in only a smaller share of those affected – in the majority it becomes chronic and often runs for years without noticeable symptoms, which is why many people first learn of their infection through an incidental finding. Left untreated, chronic hepatitis C can lead to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, or liver cancer. Since the introduction of modern direct-acting antiviral medications, hepatitis C can be completely cured within a few weeks in the vast majority of those affected – a decisive medical advance over the considerably more arduous therapies of the past. How an infection was acquired says nothing about the character of the person affected.
Typical symptoms: Often no or only nonspecific symptoms for years (fatigue, joint pain); Frequently an incidental diagnosis on routine blood tests; Occasional mild discomfort in the upper right abdomen; In advanced stages, signs of liver cirrhosis; Psychological strain from retrospective questions about transmission and disclosure decisions
Emergency notice: See a doctor immediately for severe jaundice, confusion, a tendency to bleed, or severe abdominal pain – these can indicate a serious liver complication.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
How a chronic hepatitis C infection was acquired carries no significance for this psychosomatic reflection and no moral judgment whatsoever – instead, this is about the often years-long road to diagnosis, the decision of who to tell, treatment discipline during the weeks of therapy, and the handling of closeness and intimacy throughout. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle the incidental finding, the chance of a cure, and their own history before it.
--- Type 1: The One ---
SE1: After the incidental finding, the self-preservation One often searches her past for a mistake she could have avoided, rather than simply taking the diagnosis for what it is. This retrospective self-interrogation can weigh on her more heavily than the illness itself.
SO1: Whether she should have informed others is something the social One thinks through carefully as soon as she learns of the diagnosis, guiding herself strictly by what she considers ethically required. This sense of duty can bring relief, as long as it doesn't tip into excessive self-condemnation.
SX1: Toward the one important person, the sexual One wants to handle the diagnosis with particular correctness and honesty, even if that means allowing uncomfortable questions about her own past.
--- Type 2: The Two ---
SE2: During the several weeks of therapy, the self-preservation Two often worries more about the practical needs of her family than about her own recovery. Consciously giving herself priority during these weeks is especially hard for her.
SO2: Whom to tell about the diagnosis is a choice the social Two makes very carefully within her wide circle of acquaintances, worried she might be seen as less helpful once she herself needs support.
SX2: The sexual Two usually confides openly in the one close person, and during the treatment weeks actually allows herself to be cared for, rather than continuing to be there primarily for others.
--- Type 3: The Three ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three handles the therapy with discipline, like another project with a clear timeline toward a cure, which suits her well given the comparatively short duration of modern treatment.
SO3: The social Three prefers not to speak about the diagnosis at all in her professional environment, worried her flawless image might take a hit. Sometimes she mentions it retrospectively, only once the cure is complete.
SX3: Only once she feels secure enough in the relationship does the sexual Three reveal herself to the person for whom she wants to present as attractive. This calculated openness differs from the sustained concealment of the other Three variants.
--- Type 4: The Four ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four, the counter-type, gets through treatment tenaciously and quietly, without openly showing her own exhaustion.
SO4: The social Four may see the diagnosis as further proof of an especially hard life path, which can distract from the actually good chance of a cure with modern therapies.
SX4: With great emotional openness, the sexual Four shares the diagnosis within the one deep relationship, carrying the hope of being fully understood especially in this vulnerable phase.
--- Type 5: The Five ---
SE5: Before allowing herself to engage emotionally with the diagnosis, the self-preservation Five thoroughly gathers all available information on genotype, treatment options, and cure rates. This knowledge restores her sense of control.
SO5: The social Five prefers exchanging views with other affected people in specialist forums over speaking about the diagnosis with those directly around her. This abstract exchange yields insight, but doesn't replace personal closeness.
SX5: She researches the changed urinary diversion in purely factual terms at first, almost like a technical problem – only within her one deep bond does the sexual Five allow herself to admit it also shames her.
--- Type 6: The Six ---
SE6: The high cure rate of modern therapies can give the self-preservation Six a great deal of security once she has informed herself thoroughly. Still, a certain underlying tension often remains until the follow-up test confirms the cure.
SO6: What her treatment team says becomes the social Six's touchstone, and she seeks additional exchange with other affected people, to feel more secure within community.
SX6: The sexual Six, the counter-type, handles the diagnosis in a strikingly proactive way – she informs herself actively, pursues treatment promptly, and tackles the topic head-on rather than pushing it aside.
--- Type 7: The Seven ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven readily experiences the several weeks of therapy as a restriction on her accustomed lightness, and tends to push checkup appointments aside in favor of more pleasant plans.
SO7: The social Seven, the counter-type, hardly ever puts her own concerns above her commitment to others – not even her own treatment. Seeing the therapy through consistently, rather than neglecting it along the way, is a deliberate practice for her.
SX7: The sexual Seven tends not to mention her diagnosis in passing across many contacts – she shows openness about it and about the treatment in a focused way, only within the one especially meaningful relationship.
--- Type 8: The Eight ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight actively steers her own treatment, informs herself, compares options, and refuses to be passively pushed through the healthcare system. This self-determination gives her security.
SO8: The social Eight wants to appear unbroken and strong within the group even during treatment – an open admission of exhaustion contradicts her self-image as protector.
SX8: The sexual Eight watches over her partner's changed body almost as closely as her own – with her own diagnosis, this relationship uncomfortably reverses, and that reversal is rarely something she brings up openly.
--- Type 9: The Nine ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine wants her daily routine to continue as undisturbed as possible by the treatment, which can make checkup appointments easy to lose track of. An outside nudge helps her actively pursue her own recovery.
SO9: So as not to burden anyone around her, the social Nine often keeps her diagnosis quiet for a long time, even when an open conversation could bring her support.
SX9: Whether her partner reacts calmly and supportively matters more to the sexual Nine when disclosing than her own feelings about it. When that reaction turns out positive, she too can accept the treatment more easily.
Chronic hepatitis C says nothing about a person's character or way of life, regardless of how it was acquired, and today it is curable in the vast majority of those affected. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes handles the incidental finding, treatment discipline, and their own disclosure differently – some through knowledge, others through control, care for others, or selective trust. This knowledge does not replace antiviral treatment, but can help, alongside it, to understand why people with the same diagnosis cope so differently.

HIV / AIDS (Psychosomatics Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A diagnosis that today, with modern treatment, allows for a normal, long life – and yet remains bound up with deep-seated social stigma to this day.
Definition: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a virus that specifically attacks certain cells of the immune system and, left untreated, can lead over years to their progressive weakening, until the stage of AIDS is reached, in which the body can no longer build adequate defenses even against normally harmless pathogens. Transmission occurs through certain bodily fluids, most commonly through unprotected sexual contact or shared needles. Since the 1990s, treatment has been fundamentally transformed by antiretroviral therapy (ART): with regular use of modern medications, the amount of virus in the blood can be reduced to the point of being undetectable – those affected thereby achieve a nearly normal life expectancy and can no longer transmit the virus sexually (›Undetectable = Untransmittable‹). HIV is thus, for people with access to treatment, a well-manageable chronic condition today, not a death sentence. How an infection was acquired says nothing about the character of the person affected, and the social stigma still widely attached to those affected bears no relation to the actual medical risk under treatment.
Typical symptoms: Often flu-like symptoms shortly after infection, which are easily overlooked; Frequently no or only nonspecific symptoms for years without treatment; In the advanced, untreated stage, recurring infections due to weakened immune defenses; Under effective therapy, usually no disease-related symptoms; Considerable psychological strain from the shock of diagnosis, stigma experience, and disclosure decisions
Emergency notice: See a doctor promptly if an acute HIV infection is suspected, or with a known infection and a sudden cluster of unusually severe infectious illnesses.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
How an HIV infection was acquired carries absolutely no significance for this psychosomatic reflection and no moral judgment whatsoever – this is exclusively about how a person handles the shock of diagnosis, the question of who to confide in and who not, lifelong treatment adherence, and the navigation of closeness, intimacy, and partnership after the diagnosis. The social stigma that continues to accompany HIV to this day is itself an independent psychological burden, separate from the medical course of the disease. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle disclosure, treatment discipline, and their own vulnerability toward others.
--- Type 1: The One ---
SE1: The self-preservation One keeps to her daily medication with great discipline, which gives her inner steadiness. What weighs more heavily is often an inner judge who wrongly interprets the diagnosis as a moral failing of her own, though there is no basis for that whatsoever.
SO1: To whom a duty of disclosure applies is something the social One thinks through with particular thoroughness given this transmissible diagnosis, guiding herself strictly by what she considers ethically required. This clear rulebook can bring relief, as long as it doesn't tip into excessive self-condemnation.
SX1: Within the one important partnership, the sexual One searches for exactly the right, honest way to handle disclosure, often accompanied by worry that she might not appear fully morally upstanding within this one relationship.
--- Type 2: The Two ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two often continues caring for her family unchanged after the diagnosis, while keeping her own neediness as small as possible. Allowing herself as much care as she gives others is a deliberate learning task for her.
SO2: Within her wide network, the social Two chooses very carefully whom to tell about the diagnosis, out of deeply rooted fear of rejection through stigma. This selectivity can protect her, but can also isolate her severely.
SX2: The sexual Two genuinely lets herself be cared for by this one particular person, rather than continuing to be there primarily for others. This mutual care can become a sustaining resource.
--- Type 3: The Three ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three carries out her treatment with discipline and routine, as just another functional building block of her day. About the diagnosis itself, she speaks with almost no one.
SO3: The social Three sees her flawless public image threatened by the stigma surrounding this diagnosis, which is why she often tells no one in her professional environment for a lifetime. Maintaining this facade costs considerable inner energy.
SX3: A calculated timing governs when the sexual Three reveals the diagnosis: only once the relationship with the person for whom she unfolds her charm seems solid enough. This differs from the ongoing concealment of the other Three variants.
--- Type 4: The Four ---
SE4: Without much fuss, the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, simply carries on with her diagnosis, while quietly the feeling deepens that she must constantly fight against something in daily life.
SO4: That of being judged especially harshly and unfairly by society – this feeling can find confirmation for the social Four through the stigma surrounding HIV, within her life story. Framing it this way can build solidarity with others affected, but can also entrench her own suffering.
SX4: With great emotional intensity, and the hope of being fully accepted precisely in this vulnerability, the sexual Four reveals the diagnosis within the one deep relationship. If that openness is met, it can become one of the closest bonds of her life.
--- Type 5: The Five ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five thoroughly gathers all available facts on transmission routes, treatment, and prognosis in order to meet the diagnosis with knowledge instead of diffuse fear. This knowledge can be reassuring, but doesn't replace talking about her own feelings.
SO5: The social Five can engage abstractly in professional or activist communities around HIV, without revealing herself within her close personal circle. This exchange yields valuable knowledge, but doesn't replace personal closeness.
SX5: About the possible loss of fertility, the sexual Five first thinks in facts and options rather than feelings – the actual grief underneath, she usually only allows herself within her one deep bond.
--- Type 6: The Six ---
SE6: The self-preservation Six handles her daily medication and regular checkups with great care, at least to have reliable certainty here. Familiarizing herself with the fact that the viral load becomes undetectable under therapy can noticeably ease her uncertainty.
SO6: The social Six orients herself by her treatment team's statements and by support groups, to find security in dealing with the diagnosis. Shared exchange with other affected people can be especially effective at reducing her fear of stigma.
SX6: The sexual Six, the counter-type, reacts to the diagnosis with courage rather than fear – she informs herself actively, brings the topic up openly within the one important relationship, and refuses to be silenced by social stigma.
--- Type 7: The Seven ---
SE7: Her accustomed lightness is something the self-preservation Seven doesn't want a diagnosis to take away, so she gladly postpones dealing with it seriously. Regular checkup appointments can easily slip out of view as a result.
SO7: The social Seven, the counter-type, readily hides her own burden behind continued activity for others. Actually addressing the diagnosis, rather than covering it over this way, is a deliberate practice for her.
SX7: Rather than mentioning her diagnosis in passing, the sexual Seven opens up about it deliberately within the one especially meaningful relationship. This focused approach can create a sustainable, protected closeness.
--- Type 8: The Eight ---
SE8: When, to whom, and how she tells people about the diagnosis is something the self-preservation Eight decides entirely on her own, refusing to let anyone take this control over her own story away from her. This self-determination can give her security where stigma silences others.
SO8: Admitting vulnerability contradicts the social Eight's self-image as protector of her group, which is why she initially wants to keep showing strength with this diagnosis. Some social Eights become especially effective advocates against the stigma precisely once they openly acknowledge it.
SX8: Power and closeness get negotiated by the sexual Eight in her one intense bond often through the body rather than words – fear of the disease progressing shifts this quiet contest of strength without her ever naming it out loud.
--- Type 9: The Nine ---
SE9: Barely changed by the diagnosis is how the self-preservation Nine wants her daily life to remain, which can make treatment appointments easy to lose track of. An outside nudge helps her keep her own health actively in view.
SO9: To avoid conflict or rejection through stigma, the social Nine often keeps her diagnosis quiet for years, even from her closest friends. Setting her own situation aside like this can cost her badly needed support.
SX9: Understanding and closeness from her partner, rather than withdrawal, can noticeably ease the sexual Nine's fear around the diagnosis – his reaction often weighs more heavily for her than her own initial processing of it.
An HIV diagnosis says nothing about a person's character or way of life, regardless of how it was acquired – and under modern treatment it is today a well-manageable chronic condition with a nearly normal life expectancy. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes handles disclosure, treatment adherence, and social stigma differently – some through knowledge, others through control, selective trust, or active advocacy. This knowledge does not replace antiretroviral treatment, but can help, alongside it, to understand why people with the same diagnosis cope so differently.

Tuberculosis (Psychosomatics Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A bacterial infection that mainly affects the lungs and demands weeks to months of isolation and treatment adherence.
Definition: Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which primarily affects the lungs but can in principle involve other organs as well. Transmission occurs through airborne droplets when coughing, usually with close and prolonged contact. Not every infection leads to active disease – in many people, the bacterium remains in an inactive, latent form in the body for years without causing symptoms. When the disease does become active, it is generally curable with a several-months combination therapy of multiple antibiotics, though this requires a high degree of treatment adherence throughout, since an interrupted course of therapy can lead to resistance. During the contagious phase, temporary isolation is also necessary to prevent further spread.
Typical symptoms: Persistent cough lasting more than three weeks, sometimes with traces of blood; Night sweats and gradual weight loss; Ongoing fatigue and loss of appetite; Mild fever over an extended period; Chest pain when breathing or coughing
Emergency notice: See a doctor immediately for severe coughing up of blood or severe shortness of breath.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Tuberculosis confronts those affected with an unusual double demand: months of uninterrupted treatment adherence, and, during the contagious phase, an enforced isolation from precisely the people who would otherwise provide support. In TCM, such a state is often interpreted as a deep-seated weakness of Lung Yin, associated with inner restlessness and a gradual loss of vitality. Psychosomatically, tuberculosis often reads as an image of forced slowing down and separation that fundamentally contradicts one's own life rhythm. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle the long duration of treatment and the temporary isolation.
--- Type 1: The One ---
SE1: The self-preservation One takes the months-long antibiotic combination with great precision through to the prescribed final day, even once symptoms have long since improved. This consistency protects her especially reliably against resistance.
SO1: The social One takes her isolation obligation during the contagious phase particularly seriously, out of a feeling that she would otherwise be carelessly endangering others. This strict self-discipline can somewhat ease the forced separation from others for her.
SX1: The sexual One explains the necessity of isolation carefully and conscientiously to the one person she is closely bonded to, so no misunderstanding arises about the temporary nature of the separation.
--- Type 2: The Two ---
SE2: Offering practical help to her family is scarcely possible for the self-preservation Two during the isolation phase, which can weigh on her especially heavily. Finding ways to stay caring from a distance helps her get through this time.
SO2: Being unreachable for her wide network of contacts feels to the social Two like a particularly painful loss of her usual role during isolation. Digital closeness can at least partly offset this loss.
SX2: Being physically separated from the one important person hits the sexual Two especially hard, since it is precisely that one bond that otherwise gives her stability. Regular direct contact, even if only from a distance, becomes especially important to her.
--- Type 3: The Three ---
SE3: Her usual capacity to function in daily life is significantly limited during treatment and isolation, which the self-preservation Three finds especially hard to accept. Framing the therapy itself as a clearly structured project can help her get through this phase.
SO3: The isolation phase inevitably interrupts the social Three's visible public engagement, which she experiences as a particularly uncomfortable standstill. She tends to downplay the illness to others.
