SX3: The sexual Three is most likely to show her exhaustion during treatment to the one person especially important to her, rather than continuing to appear flawless. This protected space can actually support recovery more than a maintained facade would.
--- Type 4: The Four ---
SE4: Tenaciously and mostly without much fuss, the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, gets through her isolation phase, while quietly it deepens her sense of always standing somewhat outside things anyway.
SO4: That of being hit especially hard by life – this familiar feeling can intensify for the social Four through the forced separation during the contagious phase. Dwelling in this sense of isolation can hold recovery back rather than advance it.
SX4: The sexual Four often writes especially intense, emotional messages to the one meaningful person during isolation, to make up for the physical separation through emotional closeness.
--- Type 5: The Five ---
SE5: The enforced isolation phase can, paradoxically, be less burdensome for the self-preservation Five than for others, since it suits her existing need for withdrawal and protected reserves.
SO5: The social Five thoroughly gathers expert knowledge on the disease and its treatment, which during the isolation phase also allows her an abstract exchange with other affected people in specialist forums.
SX5: Fertility and sexuality are topics the sexual Five rarely discusses even under ordinary circumstances – a diagnosis touching exactly that can deepen this reticence further, except toward the one person she truly opens up to.
--- Type 6: The Six ---
SE6: Taking her medication on a precise schedule gives the self-preservation Six an important sense of security and control over her own healing process during the long course of treatment.
SO6: The social Six orients herself very precisely by the clear instructions of her treatment team during therapy, which gives her security in a situation she finds unsettling.
SX6: The sexual Six, the counter-type, answers her uncertainty during the isolation phase with active engagement – she seeks out occupation, informs herself, and stays in motion, rather than lingering in worry.
--- Type 7: The Seven ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven especially misses her usual freedom of movement and open possibilities during the isolation phase. Finding small new pleasures within her own four walls helps her get through this time.
SO7: The social Seven, the counter-type, cannot maintain her usual commitment to others during isolation as she otherwise would, which can trigger an inner conflict between forced passivity and her habitual engagement.
SX7: The sexual Seven concentrates her energy during isolation on the one connection that still remains possible, usually maintained across a distance, rather than holding onto many contacts at once.
--- Type 8: The Eight ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight normally keeps full control over her daily life and freedom of movement. An externally imposed isolation can be especially hard for her to bear, since it shakes her fundamental sense of autonomy.
SO8: The social Eight wants to remain consistently present and strong for her group, and a forced retreat due to isolation requirements barely fits this self-image. This stance can trigger particularly strong resistance in her.
SX8: Possession and bonding are closely linked for the sexual Eight in her one important relationship – the fear of feeling less desirable to her partner after a possible loss of fertility usually stays her own, unspoken struggle.
--- Type 9: The Nine ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine often accepts her isolation phase with surprising equanimity and adapts to the changed routine, while inner restlessness about the long separation from her familiar surroundings is easily overlooked.
SO9: The social Nine gladly sets aside her own burden from isolation within the group, so as not to trouble anyone with her changed situation. This setting-aside can prevent her from getting the emotional support she actually needs.
SX9: If her partner stays composed during the separation, the sexual Nine orients herself by that more than by her own burden – which can allow her own exhaustion from the isolation to go unnoticed for an especially long time.
No one is immune to tuberculosis, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes handles the long treatment duration and temporary isolation in its own way – some through strict discipline, others through withdrawal, care from a distance, or active action against their own restlessness. This knowledge does not replace antibiotic treatment, but can help, alongside it, to understand why people respond so differently to the same diagnosis.

Lyme Disease (from Tick Bites) (Psychosomatics Register · Immune System & Autoimmune)
A bacterial infection following a tick bite, usually well treatable when caught early, but able to progress insidiously if left untreated.
Definition: Lyme disease is an infectious disease caused by bacteria of the genus Borrelia, transmitted through the bite of an infected tick. A typical, though not universal, early sign is erythema migrans, a ring-shaped skin rash spreading outward from the bite site. Left untreated, the infection can spread after weeks to months to the joints, the nervous system, or the heart, causing varied and sometimes hard-to-place symptoms there. When caught early, Lyme disease is generally well treatable with a course of antibiotics usually lasting two to four weeks. Because symptoms can vary so widely and a tick bite often goes unnoticed, diagnosis is sometimes made only after a prolonged phase of nonspecific complaints.
Typical symptoms: Erythema migrans around the bite site in the first days to weeks (not present in everyone affected); Flu-like symptoms such as fatigue, headache, and body aches; In later stages, joint pain and swelling, especially in large joints; Nerve pain, paralysis symptoms, or sensory disturbances with neurological involvement; Heart rhythm disturbances with rare cardiac involvement
Emergency notice: See a doctor promptly for acute paralysis symptoms, severe nerve pain, or heart rhythm disturbances.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Lyme disease often strikes people unexpectedly out of an entirely ordinary everyday situation – a walk, gardening, an outing in nature – without any basis for implying carelessness. Precisely because the bite itself often goes unnoticed and symptoms can develop gradually and ambiguously, the illness confronts those affected with the particular challenge of facing a diffuse, hard-to-grasp set of complaints. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct pattern emerges in how they handle this ambiguity between early suspicion, delayed diagnosis, and treatment.
--- Type 1: The One ---
SE1: After a tick bite, the self-preservation One checks the bite site with great care over days and weeks, so as not to miss any sign of a spreading rash. This thoroughness can considerably favor early treatment.
SO1: The social One informs herself precisely about the right precautions against tick bites and happily passes this knowledge on to others too, from a sense of carrying a certain responsibility for the group's wellbeing.
SX1: After a shared outing in nature, the sexual One conscientiously alerts her important companion to possible tick bites, out of genuine concern for their health, not out of excessive anxiety.
--- Type 2: The Two ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two often doesn't take her nonspecific early symptoms seriously enough, because practical tasks for her family seem more important to her than her own diffuse exhaustion. This setting-aside can needlessly delay diagnosis.
SO2: Describing her hard-to-pin-down symptoms is difficult for the social Two within her large circle of acquaintances, since she dislikes being seen as someone constantly complaining about unclear ailments.
SX2: The sexual Two describes her diffuse symptoms to the one important person openly and in detail, which often prompts that person to push together for a medical workup.
--- Type 3: The Three ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three long attributes her creeping exhaustion to overwork or lack of sleep rather than considering an infection, since any decline in her own capacity to function contradicts her self-image.
SO3: Diffuse symptoms that resist clear description hardly fit the high-performing image the social Three cultivates in her professional environment, which is why she is reluctant to talk about them. This reticence can delay early diagnosis.
SX3: The sexual Three usually keeps her exhaustion hidden from her professional environment but admits it to the one person for whom she wants to remain especially present, which can favor an early joint workup.
--- Type 4: The Four ---
SE4: The self-preservation Four, the counter-type, endures her diffuse symptoms tenaciously and without much fuss, which can actually make an early workup harder, since she downplays her own suffering.
SO4: That of not really being understood by doctors and those around her – this feeling finds easy confirmation for the social Four in the often difficult, delayed diagnosis of Lyme disease, precisely because the symptoms are so varied and hard to grasp.
SX4: With great emotional precision, the sexual Four describes her diffuse symptoms to the one deep relationship, which can help that person actually grasp the extent of the burden.
--- Type 5: The Five ---
SE5: As soon as she suspects an infection, the self-preservation Five thoroughly gathers all available information on symptoms, diagnostics, and treatment for Lyme disease. This knowledge can help drive forward an often difficult diagnosis herself.
SO5: The social Five happily researches specialist forums on Lyme disease and its many possible courses before speaking about her symptoms within her immediate circle. This abstract exchange yields knowledge, but doesn't replace direct conversation with her treatment team.
SX5: Researching the course of the illness gives the sexual Five a sense of control she otherwise often lacks – the actual fear behind it, she shows almost no one but the one person who truly knows her.
--- Type 6: The Six ---
SE6: After noticing a tick bite, the self-preservation Six observes the bite site and her own condition very closely, out of a legitimate need for early certainty about her state.
SO6: Ambiguous statements about her diffuse symptoms can be especially unsettling for the social Six, since a Lyme disease diagnosis sometimes takes several attempts. Exchange with other affected people in relevant groups can restore her sense of security.
SX6: Rather than settling for an unsatisfying answer, the sexual Six, the counter-type, meets her uncertainty about unclear symptoms with active forward motion – she seeks out several medical opinions instead.
--- Type 7: The Seven ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven long interprets her creeping exhaustion as a temporary slump that will pass on its own, rather than fitting a medical workup into her otherwise densely packed plans.
SO7: In favor of her continued commitment to others, the social Seven, the counter-type, readily overlooks her unclear symptoms. Taking these diffuse symptoms seriously anyway is a deliberate practice for her.
SX7: The sexual Seven speaks most openly about her own symptoms within the one especially meaningful relationship, which tends to prompt that person to push for a joint workup rather than her doing it alone.
--- Type 8: The Eight ---
SE8: A creeping, hard-to-grasp exhaustion without a clear opponent is especially hard for the self-preservation Eight to bear, since she is accustomed to tackling problems head-on. A clear diagnosis, once it arrives, can paradoxically bring her relief, because she can finally act again.
SO8: Even with diffuse symptoms, the social Eight wants to remain consistently strong and present for her group – admitting unclear exhaustion barely fits her self-image. This stance can delay early evaluation.
SX8: Jealously, the sexual Eight normally guards any attention that might threaten her bond from outside – with a progressive illness like this, that same vigilance turns unexpectedly against her own mortality, something she rarely puts into words.
--- Type 9: The Nine ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine often becomes consciously aware of her creeping early symptoms only late, so absorbed is she in her familiar routine. An outside nudge, for instance from people close to her, can help her take her own situation seriously at all.
SO9: The social Nine gladly sets her own diffuse symptoms aside within the group, so as not to burden anyone with a still-unclear picture. This setting-aside can considerably delay an early workup.
SX9: Whether her partner even notices a change and brings it up can, for the sexual Nine with diffuse symptoms, provide the decisive prompt toward evaluation – more than her own, often unclear, sense of it.
No one is immune to Lyme disease, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict on a lack of caution in nature. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes handles the ambiguity of early symptoms and the road to diagnosis differently – some through careful observation, others through research, restraint, or trust placed in someone close. This knowledge does not replace antibiotic treatment, but can help, alongside it, to understand why people respond so differently to the same diffuse set of complaints.

Anorexia Nervosa (Psychosomatics Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
An eating disorder in which control over one's own body becomes the central source of stability, while the danger to life and health is pushed aside.
Definition: Anorexia nervosa is a serious eating disorder in which those affected restrict their eating so severely that a markedly low body weight results for their age, height, and build – accompanied by a pronounced fear of weight gain and a distorted perception of one's own body. Self-worth is closely tied to weight and body shape in this illness. Anorexia nervosa is considered one of the mental illnesses with the highest health risks, because it affects the entire organism – the cardiovascular system, hormone balance, bone density. Neurobiologically, genetic predisposition, personality factors such as perfectionism, family and social influences, and often a triggering life event all play a role together. Early, specialized treatment significantly improves the prognosis.
Typical symptoms: Significant weight loss through restricted eating; Pronounced fear of weight gain despite being underweight; Distorted perception of one's own body; Intense preoccupation with food, weight, and body image; Withdrawal from social situations, especially around shared meals; Physical exhaustion and difficulty concentrating; Absence of menstruation in affected women
Emergency notice: In cases of severe underweight, circulatory problems, cardiac arrhythmia, or other physical warning signs, immediate medical evaluation is necessary – anorexia nervosa can have life-threatening physical consequences. Likewise, in the case of suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately or call emergency services. Specialized eating-disorder treatment should be sought early, not only once things reach an acute crisis.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
In anorexia nervosa, one's own body becomes the last place where control still seems possible, while much else feels uncontrollable all around. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an inner battle for stability, worth, and self-determination that – for reasons that differ from subtype to subtype – discharges specifically around food. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern can underlie this struggle.
--- Type 1: A Discipline That Allows No Exception ---
SE1: Fixed rules hold the self-preservation One's daily life together, and it is precisely around food that this rule-bound quality can turn into a crushing strictness that barely permits exceptions anymore. Her own body becomes a testing ground for a rightness that never quite feels achieved.
SO1: In front of the group, the social One wants to be seen as exemplary, and self-mastery counts among her most visible virtues. This longing for flawless self-discipline can shift unnoticed onto eating, until control becomes a substitute for recognition.
SX1: The sexual One directs her standards more outward, toward the one person or cause she wants to improve, rather than turning them solely against her own body. This externalizing tends to offer her somewhat more protection from the inward-directed strictness seen in other One variants, though the pattern cannot be entirely ruled out.
--- Type 2: A Worth Sought Through Renunciation ---
SE2: Caring for others comes more easily to the self-preservation Two than caring for herself – her own needs, including eating, easily fall by the wayside. Out of this chronic self-neglect an eating disorder can develop that stays unnoticed for a long time because outwardly it looks like selflessness.
SO2: Being indispensable to many gives the social Two her footing, and a slim, controlled body can unconsciously become another means, within her circle, of being needed and admired. Her own hunger increasingly recedes behind the image others are meant to see.
SX2: Intense closeness and affirmation are what the sexual Two seeks in the one important relationship, and the fear of not being attractive enough for her partner can translate directly into her own eating behavior. This narrowing onto a single relationship distinguishes her from the broader effort of other Two variants.
--- Type 3: An Image That Must Be Controlled ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three secures her sense of capability through concrete, measurable results, and weight can be measured with particular precision. This measurability can turn eating behavior into yet another project that never counts as finished.
SO3: How she is perceived publicly matters enormously to the social Three, and a flawlessly controlled body can become a central building block of that image. Behind the seemingly effortless self-mastery on display often lies an exhausting inner struggle that stays hidden for a long time.
SX3: To the one person who truly matters to her, the sexual Three will readily show doubt and exhaustion rather than maintaining only the flawless image. This willingness to open up can be an important first step toward seeking help, one other Three variants take less readily on their own.
--- Type 4: An Identity Defined Through the Body ---
SE4: Through persistent action, the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, processes her inner longing rather than surrendering to it passively – and this action can express itself as strict control over her own body when the underlying inner emptiness otherwise feels hard to grasp.
SO4: The social Four often carries her sense of being different visibly outward, and an extremely controlled body can – paradoxically – become an expression of that difference that sets her apart from others. The deep shame underlying it often stays unspoken.
SX4: The sexual Four actively seeks intensity in her relationship to the desired person, and the fear of not being desirable enough there can directly shape her own eating behavior. This strongly relationship-bound pattern differs from the more inwardly processed withdrawal of other Four variants.
--- Type 5: A Withdrawal That Reaches the Body Too ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five already reduces her needs consistently to the essentials in order to make do with limited resources – this pattern can carry over directly into eating, until her own hunger is barely registered as such anymore.
SO5: Through knowledge, the social Five stays connected to the world, and nutrition can become another domain she analyzes meticulously and controls rationally – until the intellectual preoccupation with food increasingly crowds out the actual, physical act of eating.
SX5: Building up expertise on values and insulin types gives the sexual Five a sense of mastering the diagnosis – how exhausting the constant management actually is, she admits mostly only to the one trusted person.
--- Type 6: A Security Sought Through Rules ---
SE6: Fixed routines give the self-preservation Six a footing in a world she experiences as uncertain, and a strictly regulated way of eating can become such a routine, promising security in a place where fear actually reigns.
SO6: The social Six is happy to orient herself by the guidelines of her group or recognized authorities, including on questions of nutrition – strict rules deemed correct from outside can unnoticeably tip into an eating disorder, because at first they look like disciplined compliance.
SX6: Active, courageous action instead of anxious retreat is how the sexual Six, the counter-type, meets her fear – this courage can express itself as a defiant, almost combative control over her own body, behind which the same insecurity hides as in other Six variants.
--- Type 7: A Lightness Meant to Cover the Pain ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven reflexively papers over unpleasant feelings with pleasant distraction – eating behavior can paradoxically tip in both directions, between controlled restriction and the attempt to fill every emptiness immediately.
SO7: The social Seven, the counter-type, permanently overrides her own needs in favor of the group – this chronic self-neglect can extend to her own eating as well, which is barely registered as a need of her own anymore.
SX7: In the intense relationship to the desired person, the sexual Seven allows even painful feelings, rather than constantly papering over them – this willingness toward honesty can help her name a developing eating disturbance earlier than other Seven variants.
--- Type 8: A Control That Allows No Weakness ---
SE8: Great severity governs how the self-preservation Eight watches over her own provisioning, and this severity can turn against her own body when controlling food becomes the last arena in which strength can be proven.
SO8: The social Eight stays strong for her group even once her own exhaustion has long been palpable – a rigidly controlled way of eating can remain unnoticed as one of the few forms of weakness she permits herself at all.
SX8: Daily insulin management is something the sexual Eight tends to treat as one more territory to master rather than a vulnerability – that same fighting spirit can keep her from accepting support in time, even from the one person she otherwise trusts completely.
--- Type 9: A Body That Makes Itself Invisible ---
SE9: The self-preservation Nine easily loses herself in habit and withdrawal, and restricted eating can settle in gradually as just another habit that goes largely unquestioned, until her own condition is barely noticed anymore.
SO9: So as not to cause a fuss, the social Nine readily sets her own needs aside within the group – this self-neglect can extend all the way to her own eating, which quietly diminishes without anyone noticing.
SX9: The sexual Nine readily adopts her partner's preferences and habits as her own once she merges with him, including around food – if she loses touch with her own hunger in the process, it can go unnoticed for a long time because it feels like adaptation.
Anorexia nervosa can affect anyone, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict or an explanation that removes responsibility. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes seeks control over its own body for its own inner reason – some through perfectionism, others through withdrawal, merging adaptation, or a chronically overridden need of their own. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outward symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance – always as a complement to specialized eating-disorder treatment, never as a substitute for it. When this life force is brought back into balance, the underlying inner struggle can more easily loosen its grip, even though the path there requires patience and professional support.

Bulimia Nervosa (Psychosomatics Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
An eating disorder in which loss of control and attempts at control alternate in a recurring cycle, usually hidden from view.
Definition: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by recurring episodes of losing control while eating, followed by behaviors intended to undo the feared weight gain. Unlike anorexia nervosa, body weight in bulimia nervosa is often within the normal range, which frequently keeps the illness invisible from the outside for a long time. Those affected usually experience the episodes as shameful and try to keep them strictly secret. Here too, self-worth is closely tied to weight and body shape. Neurobiologically and psychologically, a combination of genetic predisposition, perfectionism, difficulty with emotional regulation, and social pressure toward thinness play a role together. Left untreated, bulimia nervosa can have significant physical consequences, particularly for electrolyte balance and the cardiovascular system.
Typical symptoms: Recurring episodes of losing control while eating; Subsequent compensatory behaviors, often carried out in secret; Intense feelings of shame and guilt surrounding these episodes; Strong dependence of self-worth on weight and body shape; Frequently an inconspicuous, normal-weight outward appearance; Physical exhaustion, throat discomfort, dental damage; Social withdrawal around shared meals
Emergency notice: In the presence of physical warning signs such as cardiac arrhythmia, severe exhaustion, or circulatory problems, immediate medical evaluation is necessary – a disturbed electrolyte balance can become life-threatening. In the case of suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately or call emergency services. Specialized eating-disorder treatment should be sought early, not only once things reach an acute crisis.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Bulimia nervosa often lives a kind of double life – unremarkable on the outside, while on the inside it is shaped by a recurring alternation between losing control and desperately trying to regain it, something almost no one nearby ever notices. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an inner pressure that can no longer be contained, followed by an equally strong fear of the consequences of that loss of control. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern can underlie this swing between outbreak and retreat.
--- Type 1: An Outbreak That Contradicts Her Own Strictness ---
SE1: The self-preservation One ordinarily keeps her own rules very precisely, which is exactly why losing control around food feels especially shameful to her – the self-condemnation that follows can reinforce the cycle of outbreak and repair even further.
SO1: Appearing exemplary and composed in front of the group matters greatly to the social One, which is why she conceals any loss of control around eating with particular care. This double facade – flawless outwardly, chaotic in secret – costs a great deal of inner strength.
SX1: The sexual One carries her anger more outward than against herself, which tends to offer her somewhat more protection from the inward-directed cycle of loss of control and self-punishment that other One variants experience more often – though the pattern is not entirely excluded.
--- Type 2: A Hidden Outbreak After Constant Giving ---
SE2: Being there for others constantly costs the self-preservation Two more strength than she admits to herself – a secret loss of control around eating can become one of the few moments in which she actually thinks only of herself, followed by all the greater shame.
SO2: Appearing indispensable and lovable matters enormously to the social Two, which is why she keeps any loss of control around eating especially strictly hidden from those around her. The gap between her public image and her private experience can become increasingly burdensome.
SX2: Losing attractiveness through any loss of control is what the sexual Two fears within the one important relationship, which can tie the cycle of outbreak and subsequent compensation directly to that relationship. This narrowing onto one person differs from the broader social focus of other Two variants.
--- Type 3: A Crack in the Flawless Image ---
SE3: The self-preservation Three measures her capability partly by outward control – a loss of control around eating feels to her like a personal failure that she tries to make up for as quickly as possible through subsequent discipline.
SO3: Her public image demands constant self-mastery from the social Three – a loss of control around eating contradicts that image so fundamentally that it almost inevitably stays hidden. This very secrecy can keep the illness undetected for years.
SX3: To the one person truly close to her, the sexual Three can confide more readily than other Three variants, including about her own loss of control around eating. This willingness toward openness can be an important first step out of isolation.
--- Type 4: An Emotional Storm That Discharges Around Food ---
SE4: Through active doing, the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, processes inner tension rather than surrendering to it passively – precisely when this doing hits a limit, the held-back emotional force can discharge as a loss of control around eating.
SO4: The social Four usually names her intense feelings openly, which does not automatically mean she can also regulate them – an overwhelming inner pull can break through in her eating behavior, while the shame that follows is felt just as intensely.
SX4: Disappointment or absence of the intensity the sexual Four actively seeks in her relationship to the desired person can leave pent-up tension that discharges instead through eating behavior. This strongly relationship-bound pattern differs from the more inwardly processed pull of other Four variants.
--- Type 5: A Loss of Control in an Otherwise Controlled World ---
SE5: Strictly rationed, including food, are the resources of the self-preservation Five under normal circumstances – once this control breaks down, the ensuing loss of control can be especially intense, precisely because it deviates so sharply from her usual restraint.
SO5: The social Five keeps emotional matters mostly at a distance through rational knowledge – a binge episode can become one of the few moments in which unfiltered, uncontrolled emotion actually breaks through, which often irritates and embarrasses her.
SX5: Her own reserves of energy and attention are normally rationed very sparingly by the sexual Five – elevated blood fat levels can lead her to grant the one trusted person more access to those reserves than she usually allows anyone.
--- Type 6: A Tension That Breaks Through ---
SE6: Constant vigilance against possible dangers costs the self-preservation Six a great deal of energy – once this tension releases, it can discharge as a loss of control around eating, followed by renewed fear of the consequences of that very loss of control.
SO6: The social Six orients herself strongly by her group's expectations, including around food – deviating from these expectations in secret can add shame over the perceived rule-breaking that further reinforces the cycle.
SX6: Defiant, courageous action is how the sexual Six, the counter-type, meets her fear – this defiance can also show up in eating behavior, as a kind of rebellion against her own inner insecurity that can hardly be expressed any other way.
--- Type 7: A Search for Intensity That Goes Too Far ---
SE7: The self-preservation Seven reflexively seeks out pleasant experiences the moment something becomes uncomfortable – food can quickly become one of the most accessible forms of distraction, whose loss of control then triggers shame that in turn has to be papered over.
SO7: Her own needs stay permanently behind those of the group for the social Seven, the counter-type – a secret binge episode can become one of the few spaces in which she actually takes care of herself, even though it triggers guilt afterward.
SX7: The sexual Seven readily allows even painful feelings in the intense relationship to the desired person – this willingness toward openness can help her name a developing eating disturbance earlier than other Seven variants, who tend to sidestep it.
--- Type 8: A Control That Breaks Down in Secret ---
SE8: Weakness is something the self-preservation Eight shows almost never, not even to herself – a loss of control around eating contradicts that self-image so strongly that it is almost inevitably kept secret, which further deepens her isolation.
SO8: Even once her own exhaustion has long been palpable, the social Eight remains strong for her group – a secret binge episode can become one of the few forms in which that exhaustion actually shows, though only in private.
SX8: Building reserves and securing her own strength drives the sexual Eight more than actual concern for her health, even with elevated blood fat levels – only when the one person she trusts presses her persistently does real worry show through.
--- Type 9: A Pull That Drowns Out Her Own Voice ---
SE9: Habit and comfort are where the self-preservation Nine easily loses herself – eating can become a particularly convenient form of numbing, whose loss of control then triggers shame that in turn deepens the inertia even further.
SO9: Her own difficulties mostly stay held back within the group, since the social Nine dislikes causing a fuss – a secret loss of control around eating can go unnoticed for a long time this way, because she tells no one about it afterward either.
SX9: The sexual Nine easily loses touch with her own needs in merging with her partner – a binge episode can paradoxically become one of the few moments in which an actual, unfiltered impulse of her own breaks through.
Bulimia nervosa can affect anyone, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict or an explanation that removes responsibility. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes experiences the swing between losing control and attempting to regain it for its own inner reason – some through pent-up tension, others through hidden exhaustion, papered-over shame, or a chronically overridden need. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outward symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance – always as a complement to specialized eating-disorder treatment, never as a substitute for it. When this life force is brought back into balance, the underlying inner cycle can more easily be broken, even though the path there requires patience and professional support.

Binge Eating Disorder (Psychosomatics Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
An eating disorder in which recurring loss of control while eating, without any compensatory behavior afterward, leads to deep shame and often social withdrawal.
Definition: Binge eating disorder is characterized by recurring episodes of losing control while eating, in which a person eats substantially more in a short time than they themselves consider appropriate – without the compensatory behaviors typical of bulimia nervosa. The episodes are usually experienced as highly distressing, accompanied by strong feelings of shame and guilt, often eaten in secret and without any physical sensation of hunger. Unlike the occasional overeating that happens on special occasions, this is a recurring pattern with a clear degree of suffering. Neurobiologically and psychologically, a combination of difficulty with emotional regulation, genetic predisposition, and often a history of dieting or restrictive eating play a role. Specialized treatment can effectively break the cycle of loss of control and shame.
Typical symptoms: Recurring episodes of pronounced loss of control while eating; Eating noticeably faster than usual, often without genuine hunger; Eating until uncomfortably full; Intense feelings of shame and guilt after the episodes; Eating in secret out of embarrassment about the amount; No regular use of compensatory behaviors; Frequently accompanying depressive mood or anxiety
Emergency notice: In the case of severe depressive mood or suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately or call emergency services. If accompanying physical complaints such as severe exhaustion or circulatory problems occur, these should be medically evaluated. Specialized eating-disorder treatment should be sought early, not only once the level of suffering has already become severe.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
In binge eating disorder, the visible counter-movement that often marks bulimia nervosa is absent – what remains is the recurring loss of control itself and the deep shame that follows, often carried in silence for years. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an inner emptiness or pressure that finds no other outlet and therefore seeks a way out through food. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern can underlie this recurring loss of control.
--- Type 1: An Exhaustion After Too Much Tension ---
SE1: The self-preservation One holds her own standards together with discipline for long stretches, until at some point the tension tips over – a binge episode can then become a kind of release valve, immediately followed by harsh self-condemnation.
SO1: Appearing composed and exemplary to others matters greatly to the social One, which is why a loss of control around eating feels especially shameful. This shame often keeps her from talking about it at all, which can prolong the cycle.
SX1: Directing pressure solely against herself isn't the sexual One's style – she channels it outward instead, which tends to offer her somewhat more protection from the inward-directed pattern of other One variants – though the pattern cannot be entirely ruled out.
--- Type 2: A Caregiving That Forgets Itself ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two cares for others steadily, for herself barely at all – a binge episode can paradoxically become one of the few occasions when she actually takes something for herself, even though guilt follows immediately.
SO2: Staying indispensable to those around her costs the social Two a great deal of emotional energy that has to be compensated for somewhere – food can become a quiet, readily available form of self-soothing that she prefers to hide from others.
SX2: Enormous emotional attention gets invested in the one important relationship by the sexual Two – when the closeness she hoped for fails to materialize, the disappointment can discharge in a binge episode that stays closely tied to that one relationship.
--- Type 3: A Release Valve Behind the Smooth Facade ---
SE3: Staying efficient and functional matters enormously to the self-preservation Three – a binge episode contradicts this self-image so strongly that it is almost automatically concealed, which keeps the underlying exhaustion invisible.
SO3: Her public image demands constant self-control from the social Three – behind the flawless facade, a recurring, secret loss of control around eating can hide, unnoticed by anyone for years.
SX3: The one person truly close to her is who the sexual Three opens up to more readily than other Three variants would, including about her own binge episodes. This willingness toward openness can be an important first step out of isolation.
--- Type 4: An Inner Emptiness Meant to Be Filled ---
SE4: Active doing is how the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, processes her longing – when this doing hits a limit, the pent-up inner emptiness can break through in a binge episode, usually followed by quiet self-criticism.
SO4: Openly named, her melancholy is something the social Four rarely hides, which does not mean she can also fill the inner emptiness tied to it – eating can become an attempt to still that very emptiness for a moment.
SX4: A relationship that fails to deliver the intensity the sexual Four otherwise actively seeks can leave a longing that discharges instead through eating behavior. This relationship-bound pattern differs from the more inwardly processed pull of other Four variants.
--- Type 5: A Withdrawal That Reaches Eating Too ---
SE5: Strict rationing of her resources is normal for the self-preservation Five – once this control breaks down under exhaustion, a binge episode can follow, which she then tries to bring back under her usual control as quickly as possible.
SO5: Rational knowledge is how the social Five keeps emotional matters mostly at a distance – a binge episode can become one of the few moments in which unfiltered emotion actually breaks through, which often irritates her.
SX5: Intimate physical topics like this one the sexual Five normally keeps strictly private, often barely voiced even to herself – only with the one trusted person can this actually be discussed openly.
--- Type 6: A Tension That Seeks Food as Comfort ---
SE6: Constant vigilance costs the self-preservation Six a great deal of energy – eating can become a reliable, physically tangible form of comfort when inner tension can hardly be regulated otherwise.
SO6: Her group's expectations are what the social Six orients herself by most strongly – a secret loss of control around eating can become a rare space in which she actually owes no one an account of herself, even though shame follows afterward.
SX6: Courageous action is the sexual Six's, the counter-type's, usual answer to her fear – when this courage hits its limits, the underlying insecurity can, exceptionally, show up in eating behavior instead of being warded off outwardly.
--- Type 7: A Pleasure That Runs Out of Control ---
SE7: Pleasant experiences get sought out reflexively by the self-preservation Seven the moment something becomes uncomfortable – food can become one of the most accessible forms of pleasure, whose repeated loss of control then triggers shame that in turn has to be papered over.
SO7: Behind the needs of the group is where the social Seven's, the counter-type's, own needs permanently stay – a secret binge episode can become one of the few spaces in which she actually takes care of herself.
SX7: The sexual Seven readily allows difficult feelings in the intense relationship to the desired person – this willingness toward openness can help her name a developing pattern earlier than other Seven variants, who tend to sidestep it.
--- Type 8: An Exhaustion Meant to Stay Hidden ---
SE8: Almost never does the self-preservation Eight let weakness show – a secret binge episode can become one of the few forms in which exhaustion actually shows, even though it immediately disappears again behind her usual toughness.
SO8: Palpable as her own exhaustion may long have become, the social Eight remains strong for her group – food can become a quiet compensation no one sees, because outwardly she continues to seem unshakeable.
SX8: Nighttime bathroom trips and weakening urinary strength first register with the sexual Eight as weakness to overcome rather than something to treat – only in conversation with the one person who truly knows her does she admit it actually worries her.
--- Type 9: A Numbing That Covers Her Own Anger ---
SE9: Losing herself in habit and comfort comes easily to the self-preservation Nine – eating can become a particularly convenient form of numbing that keeps unpleasant feelings from ever becoming conscious in the first place.
SO9: Disliking any fuss, the social Nine mostly keeps her own anger held back within her group – this held-back anger can discharge unnoticed through eating behavior, while harmony continues to be maintained on the outside.
SX9: In close merging with her partner, the sexual Nine easily loses touch with her own needs – a binge episode can paradoxically become one of the few moments in which an actual, unfiltered impulse of her own breaks through.
Binge eating disorder can affect anyone, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict or an explanation that removes responsibility. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes experiences this recurring loss of control for its own inner reason – some through pent-up exhaustion, others through hidden caregiving, papered-over anger, or an inner emptiness that seeks to be filled briefly. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outward symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance – always as a complement to specialized eating-disorder treatment, never as a substitute for it. When this life force is brought back into balance, the underlying inner pressure can more easily be regulated, even though the path there requires patience and professional support.

Alcohol Use Disorder (Psychosomatics Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A recognized, treatable addictive illness in which alcohol increasingly becomes the only reliable way to regulate inner states.
Definition: Alcohol use disorder is a recognized psychological and physical illness, not a question of character weakness or lack of discipline. It is marked by a strong, often difficult-to-control craving for alcohol, an increasing loss of control over the amount and frequency of consumption, tolerance development, and physical withdrawal symptoms upon stopping. Consumption continues despite clearly recognizable negative consequences for health, relationships, and daily life. Neurobiologically, chronic alcohol use lastingly alters the brain's reward system, which turns the illness from a conscious decision into a distinct medical condition. The dependency often functions as a form of self-medication – an attempt to cope with fear, tension, loneliness, or emotional pain. Successful treatment addresses both the physical and psychological dimensions of the illness.
Typical symptoms: Strong, difficult-to-control craving for alcohol; Loss of control over the amount and frequency of consumption; Tolerance development requiring increasing amounts; Physical withdrawal symptoms upon stopping; Continued consumption despite clearly recognizable negative consequences; Neglect of previous interests and social contacts; Increasing preoccupation with obtaining and consuming alcohol
Emergency notice: Suddenly stopping alcohol on one's own after a long period of severe dependency can be medically dangerous – withdrawal symptoms such as severe tremors, confusion, seizures, or circulatory problems require medical supervision, in a hospital setting if in doubt. Withdrawal should therefore, where possible, take place under medical guidance rather than alone. In the case of suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately or call emergency services. Addiction counseling services offer a low-threshold, confidential first point of contact.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Alcohol use disorder rarely begins as a conscious decision – it usually creeps in over years as a seemingly reliable means of coping with tension, loneliness, or pain, until reaching for the glass becomes a distinct illness beyond one's own control. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an emotional regulation system that came to depend on a chemical shortcut because another path stayed inaccessible for a long time. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern shows what inner tension is meant to be numbed here – and a distinct possible way back.
--- Type 1: A Tension Seeking Release ---
SE1: Her own strict standards constantly cost the self-preservation One self-discipline – alcohol can become one of the few ways for her to actually let go of this inner tension at all, which makes reaching for the glass especially hard to control once it becomes habitual.
SO1: In front of her group, the social One mostly keeps mistakes and weaknesses consistently held back – drinking in secret can become an area where she feels unobserved, while the facade of control persists outwardly.
SX1: Anger gets carried more directly outward by the sexual One rather than turned against herself – this more direct way of handling tension tends to offer her somewhat more protection from the inward-directed tension of other One variants, though this is no protection against developing an addiction.
--- Type 2: An Exhaustion No One Is Meant to See ---
SE2: The self-preservation Two barely admits to herself how exhausting it is to constantly care for others – a glass in the evening can at first feel like a small, well-earned reward before it unnoticeably turns into a regular pattern.
SO2: Remaining indispensable to many costs the social Two an enormous amount of emotional energy – alcohol can become a quiet counterbalance she hides from those around her, because it doesn't fit her caring self-image at all.
SX2: When the closeness she hoped for fails to materialize in the one important relationship in which the sexual Two invests enormous emotional attention, alcohol can become a way to make that disappointment more bearable in the short term.
--- Type 3: A Facade Behind Which Exhaustion Hides ---
SE3: Staying functional and efficient matters enormously to the self-preservation Three – alcohol can initially seem like a way to wind down quickly after an exhausting day, before it turns into a pattern beyond her own control.
SO3: Her flawless public image demands constant self-mastery from the social Three – growing alcohol use contradicts that image so fundamentally that it usually stays hidden for a particularly long time, until the facade begins to crack.
SX3: More than other Three variants, the sexual Three tends to confide in the one person truly close to her, including about her own consumption. This willingness toward openness can be an important first step toward seeking help.
--- Type 4: A Longing Meant to Be Numbed ---
SE4: When the persistent doing with which the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, otherwise processes her inner longing hits a limit, alcohol can become a way to temporarily numb the held-back emotional weight.
SO4: The social Four knows her melancholy well and names it openly – alcohol can paradoxically become an amplifier of this intense emotional world rather than a relief from it, which makes her use hard to gauge.
SX4: An absent sense of intensity in her relationship to the desired person, the very thing the sexual Four otherwise actively seeks, can leave a void that alcohol becomes a substitute for briefly filling.
--- Type 5: A Withdrawal Reinforced Chemically ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five already reduces contact with others consistently – drinking alone at home can become a quiet, inconspicuous habit that develops over years without her social circle even noticing.
SO5: The social Five stays connected to the world mainly through knowledge, keeping emotional closeness at a distance – alcohol in company can at first serve as a kind of social bridge before it turns into a pattern of its own.
SX5: Fading eyesight is something the sexual Five first observes analytically rather than with concern – actually letting it worry her tends to happen only in conversation with the one trusted person.
--- Type 6: A Fear That Falls Silent for a While ---
SE6: A baseline feeling of insecurity accompanies the self-preservation Six for years at a time – alcohol can become one of the few means that actually silences this tension, which makes it especially hard to let go of again.
SO6: The social Six finds her footing mainly in her group – drinking together can at first feel like an expression of that belonging, before consumption becomes untethered from any social occasion.
SX6: Active, courageous action is how the sexual Six, the counter-type, meets her insecurity – when this courage hits its limits, alcohol can become a way to drown out the underlying fear anyway.
--- Type 7: A Search for Intensity That Tips Over ---
SE7: Unpleasant feelings get papered over reflexively by the self-preservation Seven with the next pleasant distraction – alcohol fits this pattern well and can therefore develop into a fixed habit especially quickly, before the loss of control is even consciously registered.
SO7: Favoring the group over her own needs is a permanent pattern for the social Seven, the counter-type – alcohol in company can become one of the few spaces where she actually treats herself to something, which makes it easy to underestimate her consumption.
SX7: The sexual Seven allows even painful feelings in the intense relationship to the desired person, rather than constantly papering over them – this willingness toward openness can help her name problematic use earlier than other Seven variants.
--- Type 8: A Control That Dissolves in Consumption ---
SE8: The self-preservation Eight shows weakness almost never – alcohol can become one of the few permitted spaces in which she actually lets herself go, which makes the transition from occasional use to dependency especially inconspicuous.
SO8: The social Eight barely admits to exhausted strength as long as her group still needs her – alcohol can become a quiet way of compensating for that exhaustion without having to admit it to others.
SX8: That her vision isn't as sharp as it used to be is something the sexual Eight hides from herself for a long time – control over her own perception is part of her self-image. Only direct confrontation by the one trusted person gets her to take it seriously.
--- Type 9: A Numbing of Her Own Anger ---
SE9: Routine and comfort are where the self-preservation Nine easily loses herself – a glass in the evening can become a particularly convenient further habit that intensifies unnoticed over years because it belongs to an inconspicuous everyday life.
SO9: Steadily, the social Nine lets her own opinion give way to group harmony – held-back anger over this constant adapting can unnoticeably discharge through growing alcohol use, while a calm, composed surface is kept up for everyone else.
SX9: Adopting her partner's habits as her own comes easily to the sexual Nine in merging with him – if her partner drinks regularly, she may go along with this consumption unreflectively, without recognizing it as a distinct problem of her own.
Alcohol use disorder is a serious medical illness that can affect anyone, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict or a moral judgment. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes can reach for alcohol as a regulating agent for its own inner reason – some through pent-up tension, others through hidden exhaustion, numbed longing, or held-back anger. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outward symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance – always as a complement to medically supervised addiction treatment, never as a substitute for it. When this life force is brought back into balance, the path out of dependency can become easier to walk, even though it requires patience, professional support, and often several attempts.

Medication and Drug Dependence (Psychosomatics Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A recognized addictive illness in which prescription medications or illegal substances become the only reliable way to regulate inner states.
Definition: Medication and drug dependence is a recognized psychological and physical illness, not a question of character weakness. It affects both prescription substances such as painkillers, sleep aids, and sedatives, as well as illegal drugs. It is marked by a strong craving for the substance, an increasing loss of control over the amount and frequency of use, tolerance development, and physical and psychological withdrawal symptoms upon stopping. Use continues despite clearly recognizable negative consequences for health, relationships, and daily life. The dependency often develops gradually, sometimes starting from a medically legitimate prescription, or as an attempt to cope with fear, pain, exhaustion, or emotional overload. Neurobiologically, chronic use lastingly alters the brain's reward system. Successful treatment addresses both the physical and psychological dimensions of the illness.
Typical symptoms: Strong, difficult-to-control craving for the substance; Loss of control over the amount and frequency of use; Tolerance development requiring increasing doses; Physical and psychological withdrawal symptoms upon stopping; Continued use despite clearly recognizable negative consequences; Obtaining the substance from multiple doctors or unclear sources; Withdrawal from previous interests and social contacts
Emergency notice: Suddenly stopping on one's own after prolonged use, particularly of sedatives or painkillers, can be medically dangerous and should take place under medical guidance. In the case of signs of overdose (severe clouding of consciousness, respiratory depression), call emergency services immediately. In the case of suicidal thoughts, contact a crisis hotline immediately. Addiction counseling services offer a low-threshold, confidential first point of contact, even when the substance was originally medically prescribed.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Medication and drug dependence often begins not with a wish for intoxication, but with the understandable need to finally silence pain, fear, or exhaustion – until the substance itself becomes a distinct illness that escapes its original purpose. Psychosomatically, this illness often reads as the picture of an emotional regulation system that came to depend on a chemical shortcut because another path stayed inaccessible for a long time. For each of the 27 subtypes, a distinct emotional pattern shows what inner state is meant to be numbed or regulated here – and a distinct possible way back.
--- Type 1: An Exhaustion Asking for Permission ---
SE1: Her own strict standards keep the self-preservation One in constant tension – a medically prescribed sedative can at first seem like a legitimate, controlled exception, before its use unnoticeably takes on a life of its own.
SO1: Weakness is something the social One mostly keeps consistently held back from her group – secretly reaching for medication can become a hidden area that simply doesn't fit the flawless image she presents outwardly.
SX1: Rather than against herself, the sexual One directs her inner pressure more directly outward – this more direct approach tends to offer her somewhat more protection from the inward-directed tension of other One variants, though this is no protection against developing an addiction.
--- Type 2: A Self-Care That Stays Secret ---
SE2: How exhausting the constant caring for others actually is only rarely gets admitted by the self-preservation Two to herself – a painkiller or sedative can become one of the few forms in which she actually cares for herself, which makes it easy to underestimate her use.
SO2: An enormous amount of emotional energy goes into staying indispensable to many for the social Two – a medication that dampens this tension can be something she hides from those around her, because a need for retreat doesn't fit her caring self-image.
SX2: Enormous emotional attention goes into the one important relationship for the sexual Two, and when the closeness she hoped for fails to materialize, a substance can become a way to make that disappointment more bearable in the short term.
--- Type 3: A Capability Chemically Propped Up ---
SE3: Staying functional matters enormously to the self-preservation Three – stimulating or sedating substances can at first seem like a legitimate means of maintaining her capability, before the dependency takes on a life of its own.
SO3: Constant control over her flawless public image is what the social Three maintains – growing substance use contradicts that image so fundamentally that it usually stays secret for a particularly long time, until the facade begins to crack.
SX3: Compared with other Three variants, the sexual Three finds it easier to open up to the one person truly close to her, including about her own use. This willingness toward openness can be an important first step toward seeking help.
--- Type 4: A Longing Meant to Be Numbed ---
SE4: Her inner longing is otherwise processed by the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, through persistent doing – once that outlet finds no way through anymore, a substance can become a way to temporarily numb the held-back emotional weight.
SO4: The social Four is well acquainted with her melancholy and names it openly – a substance can paradoxically become an amplifier of this intense emotional world rather than a relief from it, which makes her use hard to gauge.
SX4: Relationships that don't deliver the intensity the sexual Four otherwise actively seeks with the desired person can leave a sense of emptiness that a substance becomes a substitute for briefly filling.
--- Type 5: A Withdrawal Deepened Chemically ---
SE5: Consistently kept to a minimum, contact with others is something the self-preservation Five already reduces on her own – a sedating substance can become a quiet, inconspicuous habit that deepens this withdrawal even further without her circle ever noticing.
SO5: The social Five seeks her connection to the world mainly through knowledge, keeping emotional closeness at a distance – some substances can at first let her approach emotions in a controlled way, as if from a safe distance, before a pattern of its own develops.
SX5: Strict control over her own body can give the sexual Five a sense of safety she otherwise rarely allows herself emotionally – real closeness she permits only within her one deep bond, which can reinforce this compensation further.
--- Type 6: A Fear That Falls Silent for a While ---
SE6: For years at a time, a baseline feeling of insecurity trails the self-preservation Six – a sedative can become one of the few means that actually silences this tension, which makes it especially hard to let go of again.
SO6: Mainly within her group is where the social Six finds her footing – if a doctor she trusts prescribes a substance, she usually follows that authority conscientiously, which can paradoxically make it harder to even question a developing dependency.
SX6: The sexual Six, the counter-type, responds to her insecurity with active, courageous action – when this courage hits its limits, a substance can become a way to drown out the underlying fear anyway.
--- Type 7: A Search for Intensity That Tips Over ---
SE7: Unpleasant feelings get met reflexively by the self-preservation Seven with the next pleasant distraction – fast-acting substances fit this pattern well and can therefore develop into a fixed habit especially quickly.
SO7: Placing her own needs behind those of the group is a permanent pattern for the social Seven, the counter-type – a substance can become one of the few spaces in which she actually treats herself to something, which makes it easy to underestimate her use.
SX7: The sexual Seven doesn't constantly paper over painful feelings in the intense relationship to the desired person, but allows them – this willingness toward openness can help her name problematic use earlier than other Seven variants.
--- Type 8: A Control That Dissolves in Consumption ---
SE8: Admitting weakness comes almost never to the self-preservation Eight – a substance can become one of the few permitted spaces in which she actually lets herself go, which makes the transition from occasional use to dependency especially inconspicuous.
SO8: The social Eight mostly blocks out her own exhausted strength as long as her group still needs her – a substance can become a quiet way of compensating for that exhaustion without having to admit it to others.
SX8: Distorted vision first registers with the sexual Eight as an attack on her everyday self-sufficiency, which she reflexively plays down – her real concern only surfaces once the one person who truly knows her presses persistently enough.
--- Type 9: A Numbing of Her Own Anger ---
SE9: So easily does the self-preservation Nine lose herself in routine and comfort that a numbing medication can become a particularly convenient further habit, intensifying unnoticed over years because it belongs to an inconspicuous everyday life.
SO9: Group harmony consistently wins out over the social Nine's own opinion – held-back anger over this constant adapting can unnoticeably discharge through growing substance use, while an even-keeled front stays intact for those around her.
SX9: Her partner's habits become her own with surprising ease once the sexual Nine merges with him – if her partner uses regularly, she may go along with this use unreflectively, without recognizing it as a distinct problem of her own.
Medication and drug dependence is a serious medical illness that can affect anyone, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict or a moral judgment. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes can reach for a substance as a regulating agent for its own inner reason – some through pent-up tension, others through hidden exhaustion, numbed longing, or held-back anger. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy begins: not at the outward symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance – always as a complement to medically supervised addiction treatment, never as a substitute for it. When this life force is brought back into balance, the path out of dependency can become easier to walk, even though it requires patience, professional support, and often several attempts.

Social Phobia (Social Anxiety Disorder) (Psychosomatics Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A pronounced fear of being judged by others that turns social situations into a constant examination room.
Definition: Social phobia (social anxiety disorder) is marked by a pronounced, persistent fear of social situations in which the person might be exposed to scrutiny by others – conversations, presentations, eating in company, or simply being observed. The main fear is usually acting in an embarrassing or humiliating way, or visibly showing anxiety symptoms such as blushing, trembling, or sweating. These situations are either endured with intense discomfort or consistently avoided, which can significantly limit education, career, and relationships. Neurobiologically, heightened amygdala reactivity to social cues plays a role, favored by genetic predisposition, an anxious temperament in childhood, and humiliating social experiences.
Typical symptoms: Pronounced fear of being judged and watched by others; Avoidance of social situations, or enduring them under great distress; Blushing, trembling, sweating, racing heart in social situations; Constant worry about behaving in an embarrassing way; Excessive self-monitoring during social contact; Avoidance of eye contact; Withdrawal from education, career, or social life
Emergency notice: In the event of acute suicidal thoughts or complete social isolation accompanied by despair, contact a crisis line immediately (in the US: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, call or text 988) or call emergency services.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
Someone living with social phobia enters every room containing other people as if stepping onto a stage with invisible judges seated in the audience – the inward gaze grows so loud that little room remains for genuine contact. In TCM, a state like this is often linked to a weakness of Kidney Water, which normally lends the Heart a sense of security – without it, every encounter becomes a potential danger. Psychosomatically, social phobia often reads as the image of an inner observer who scrutinizes the self more harshly than any onlooker ever would. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in what this self-scrutiny fixes on.
--- Type 1: A verdict passed before anyone else speaks ---
SE1: Long before anyone else can say a word, the self-preservation One has already combed through her own conduct and found it wanting. In social situations, this pre-emptive self-criticism can produce pronounced tension and avoidance.
SO1: Appearing beyond reproach matters enormously to the social One in groups, so the smallest deviation can feel like public exposure. This fear of one's own misstep can harden into a full-blown social phobia.
SX1: The sexual One directs her outrage over wrongdoing straight at the one person involved, rather than fearing judgment from a crowd. This directness sets her apart from the more diffuse social withdrawal of the other One variants.
--- Type 2: A fear of seeming unlovable ---
SE2: Whether she really comes across as likeable in the group is something the self-preservation Two rechecks in every encounter. If this checking stays chronically tense, a social phobia can develop from it.
SO2: In larger gatherings, the social Two wants to be liked by as many people as possible, which raises the pressure with every appearance. The fear of being rejected anyway can grow into pronounced social anxiety.
SX2: The sexual Two concentrates her attention on the one important person rather than exposing herself to the judgment of many at once. This narrow focus relieves her of the broader social anxiety that hits the other Two variants harder.
--- Type 3: A performance that could fail ---
SE3: Her achievements are meant to speak for themselves, without the self-preservation Three particularly wanting attention. If she does end up in the spotlight unintentionally, the fear of judgment can turn out surprisingly intense.
SO3: A flawless public appearance is almost mandatory for the social Three, and correspondingly great is her fear of failing at it. This fear of failure in front of an audience can sharpen into a social phobia.
SX3: The sexual Three is allowed to seem imperfect, at least in front of the one important person, instead of constantly facing public evaluation. This relief sets her apart from the broader stage-fright of the other Three variants.
--- Type 4: A difference that draws attention ---
SE4: Functioning without standing out is what the self-preservation Four, the counter-type, usually strives for in social situations. When that doesn't work, the fear of being seen as strange can take pronounced forms.
SO4: The social Four often carries her sense of being different outward on purpose, yet fears being misunderstood or exposed because of it. This ambivalence can surface as social phobia whenever real closeness is at stake.
SX4: In the intense encounter with the desired person, the sexual Four shows herself unfiltered rather than fearing judgment in a group. This direct expression sets her apart from the more diffuse social withdrawal of the other Four variants.
--- Type 5: A retreat from the stage ---
SE5: The self-preservation Five keeps social demands consistently small in order to conserve her limited resources. If she is pushed into the center of attention anyway, a pronounced social phobia can result.
SO5: The social Five feels reasonably secure in groups when expertise is the topic, but the moment personal rather than factual questions arise, tension quickly builds. This vulnerability can condense into social anxiety.
SX5: Inner tension that cannot be regulated any other way can discharge for the sexual Five through eating behavior – especially when she feels unusually exposed emotionally outside her one deep connection.
--- Type 6: A watchful eye that never rests ---
SE6: Whether she is really safe within the group is something the self-preservation Six checks continuously, reading every reaction from others immediately. This constant checking can widen into a social phobia.
SO6: Meeting her group's expectations matters enormously to the social Six, and any deviation feels risky. This worry about her own standing can show up as pronounced social anxiety.
SX6: Direct confrontation, not social withdrawal, is how the sexual Six, the counter-type, meets her insecurity. This action orientation can protect her from the avoidance that the other Six variants show more readily.
--- Type 7: A cheerfulness with tension underneath ---
SE7: Through practical sociability, the self-preservation Seven usually manages to paper over her own discomfort. Once that discomfort can no longer be papered over, pronounced social anxiety can remain behind.
SO7: Giving as much as possible to the group matters to the social Seven, the counter-type, while her own insecurity gets covered up in the process. If this facade cracks, a social phobia can become visible.
SX7: In an intense one-on-one relationship, the sexual Seven does show insecurity rather than constantly playing it off. This openness sets her apart from the hidden tension the other Seven variants carry in larger groups.
--- Type 8: A control over the impression made ---
SE8: Showing vulnerability in front of others runs deeply against the grain for the self-preservation Eight. If she ends up in a situation where she feels at others' mercy, surprisingly intense social anxiety can result.
SO8: The social Eight usually shows up fearless for her group, while consistently hiding any insecurity of her own. This hidden tension can, rarely, surface as a social phobia.
SX8: Fearlessness is the image the sexual Eight usually presents – that social situations could intimidate her at all contradicts that self-image so strongly that she plays it down rather than admits it, at least at first.
--- Type 9: A voice that isn't meant to stand out ---
SE9: Moving through social situations unnoticed suits the self-preservation Nine far better than being pushed into the center. If she's forced there anyway, pronounced social anxiety can rise up.
SO9: Subordinating her own opinion to group harmony comes more easily to the social Nine than openly voicing it. The fear of causing friction or standing out can condense into social phobia.
SX9: The sexual Nine feels socially carried when merged with her partner, but that sense of security can be missing when she's alone in larger groups. Without her partner present, social tension can markedly increase.
No one is immune to social phobia, regardless of subtype, and no pattern is a verdict. What emerges is simply that each of the 27 subtypes handles the fear of others' judgment in its own way – some through withdrawal, others through control, facade, or a chronically over-critical self-image. This is exactly where this compass's Enneagram homeopathy comes in: not at the surface symptom, but at the life force of the respective subtype that has fallen out of balance. When this life force is brought back into balance – regardless of which of the 27 subtypes is affected – the symptoms can resolve holistically instead of merely being suppressed on the surface.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) (Psychosomatics Register · Psychiatric Conditions)
A nervous system that fails to register a survived event as over, letting it live on in memories, alarm, and avoidance.
Definition: Post-traumatic stress disorder develops in response to one or more extremely distressing events – such as violence, accidents, war, sexual abuse, or natural disasters – that directly threatened one's own life or someone else's. It is marked by the involuntary reliving of the trauma through flashbacks or nightmares, pronounced avoidance of reminders, persistently heightened tension and a strong startle response, and negative changes in thinking and mood, such as guilt, emotional numbness, or an altered worldview. Symptoms usually appear within the first months after the event and, without treatment, can persist for years. Neurobiologically, a dysregulated stress axis and altered memory processing in the brain are often found, causing the trauma to be experienced not as concluded but as ongoingly present.
Typical symptoms: Involuntary reliving of the trauma (flashbacks, nightmares); Pronounced avoidance of trauma reminders; Persistent hyperarousal and an exaggerated startle response; Concentration and sleep disturbances; Emotional numbness or a sense of detachment; Negative thoughts about oneself or the world; Irritability or outbursts of anger
Emergency notice: In the event of acute suicidal thoughts, flashbacks with risk of harm to self or others, or dissociative states with loss of control, contact a crisis line immediately (in the US: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, call or text 988) or call emergency services.
Every person can get any illness, regardless of subtype. What is described here is not a diagnosis and not statistics, but psychosomatic interpretive offerings – patterns that stand out in practice, but never replace seeing a doctor or licensed health practitioner.
A trauma does not end with the event itself; it goes on living in the nervous system for as long as it hasn't truly been processed – the body keeps standing guard against a danger that is long past. In TCM, a state like this is often associated with startled Kidney Qi, which withdraws from the Heart the grounding it needs after a shock. Psychosomatically, PTSD often reads as the image of an experience too overwhelming to be integrated into one's own life story, so it keeps returning as a constant present. Each of the 27 subtypes shows its own pattern in how it deals with this unresolved experience – though it must be stressed: no subtype makes a trauma more likely, anyone can be affected by one; only the way of processing it afterward differs.
--- Type 1: An event that demands to be judged ---
SE1: After a traumatic event, the self-preservation One often searches compulsively for what should have been done differently. This endless self-examination can burden trauma processing further instead of easing it.
SO1: Whether she acted morally correctly in the distressing situation often occupies the social One long afterward. This retrospective self-condemnation can become entangled with the actual PTSD symptoms.
